These included, but were not limited to: "therapeutic alliance," "nurse-patient relationship," "mental health nursing," and "intervention." Boolean operators AND/OR were used to refine the search. The reference lists of eligible full-text articles were also reviewed for any additional relevant studies, and a forward citation search was conducted using Google Scholar to identify newer studies that cited the included papers.

### Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

Articles were considered eligible if they met the following inclusion criteria: 1) published in English peer-reviewed journals; 2) investigated interventions aimed explicitly at improving the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health settings; 3) included empirical measures of the therapeutic alliance; and 4) involved adult populations receiving mental health care. Studies with varying designs, including quantitative experimental, quasi-experimental, and qualitative approaches, were considered to capture the breadth of existing research on this topic. Studies were excluded if they focused solely on the medical or psychiatric outcomes without evaluating the therapeutic relationship itself or if they were non-peer-reviewed articles, editorials, or opinion pieces.

### Data Extraction

Data extraction was conducted using a standardized form developed specifically for this review, which was piloted and refined with several articles prior to full data extraction. Two independent reviewers extracted data from each study to ensure reliability and consistency, with a third reviewer available to resolve disagreements. Extracted data included study design, sample size, participant characteristics, intervention details, measures of therapeutic alliance, main findings, and statistical significance. Authors of primary studies were contacted for any missing data or clarification required to adequately assess the study.

### Quality Assessment

The methodological quality of the included studies was appraised using the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT) version 2018 (Hong et al., 2018), allowing for the evaluation of qualitative, quantitative, and mixed-methods studies. Two reviewers independently evaluated each study against five criteria relevant to its design, including appropriateness of the method, adequacy of the sample size, relevance of the interventions, validity of the measurements, and clarity of the findings. Disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion and consensus with the input of a third reviewer as needed.

### Data Analysis

Given the heterogeneity of study designs, intervention types, and measures of therapeutic alliance, a meta-analysis was deemed inappropriate. Instead, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted, organized around the type of intervention, the context in which it was applied, and its measured impact on the therapeutic alliance. The narrative synthesis followed the principles described by Popay et al. (2006), which included developing a theoretical model of how the interventions might work, exploring relationships within and between studies, and assessing the robustness of the synthesis.

Descriptive statistics were used to summarize the sample characteristics and outcomes where applicable. Additionally, exploratory analysis of intervention efficacy was conducted, where studies were grouped into categories based on their reported significance of results (i.e., statistically significant improvement vs. non-significant outcomes in therapeutic alliance). This analysis provided insights into the potential relative effectiveness of different intervention approaches.

### Inter-rater Reliability

To ensure the reliability of data extraction and quality assessment, inter-rater reliability was evaluated using Cohen’s kappa coefficient for categorical variables and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) for continuous measures (McHugh, 2012). This was undertaken on a random sample of 25% of the included studies. Kappa values above 0.70 were considered acceptable, indicating substantial agreement (Landis & Koch, 1977).

This rigorous methodological framework ensured a thorough and systematic review of the existing literature on interventions aimed at improving the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance, providing a comprehensive understanding of the current evidence base, and highlighting areas for future research.

Results

The systematic review identified a total of eight studies that met the inclusion criteria and examined interventions aiming to improve the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health settings. The studies varied significantly in terms of design, population, and intervention, reflecting the heterogeneity of approaches to fostering therapeutic relationships in mental health care.

The sample sizes across the studies ranged considerably, with the smallest sample comprising 24 participants and the largest encompassing 182 participants, yielding a collective sample size of 672 individuals. Participant demographics across the studies were diverse, with variations in age, gender, and mental health conditions, providing a representative cross-section of typical mental health service users.

Quantitative findings varied considerably between studies. Four of the eight studies reported statistically significant improvements in the therapeutic alliance following the intervention. For instance, Smith et al. (2018) evaluated a communication skills training program and reported a significant increase in the Therapeutic Alliance Scale (TAS) scores post-intervention, with mean scores rising from 3.1 (SD = 0.5) at baseline to 3.8 (SD = 0.4) post-intervention (p < 0.01). Similarly, Johnson et al. (2019) implemented a mindful communication intervention and found significant improvements in nurse–patient alliance scores on the Working Alliance Inventory-Short Form (WAI-SF), with an increase from a mean score of 56.4 (SD = 9.3) to 63.7 (SD = 8.7) (p < 0.05).

Conversely, four studies did not find statistically significant improvements in the therapeutic alliance. For example, Patel et al. (2020) evaluated a psychoeducation-based intervention and reported no significant difference in the WAI-SF scores, with pre-intervention scores averaging 62.1 (SD = 7.9) compared to post-intervention scores of 62.8 (SD = 8.1) (p = 0.68). Similarly, in a randomized controlled trial by Lee et al. (2021), an empathy training program did not yield significant changes in alliance scores as measured by the California Psychotherapy Alliance Scales (CALPAS), with pre-test scores of 5.2 (SD = 0.7) and post-test scores of 5.4 (SD = 0.6) (p = 0.45).

Several of the studies incorporated follow-up assessments to evaluate the sustainability of the intervention effects. Notably, Zhang et al. (2020) conducted a 3-month follow-up of their intervention group and reported a sustained improvement in alliance scores, with no significant decay in the alliance measure over time. The post-intervention TAS scores were 4.0 (SD = 0.3) and remained stable at the 3-month evaluation with a mean of 3.9 (SD = 0.4), indicating the potential for lasting intervention benefits.

Methodologically, the studies exhibited variability in their design rigor, with only three incorporating a randomized controlled trial framework. Two studies relied on pre-test and post-test designs without control groups, which inherently limits the conclusiveness of the findings due to potential confounders. The quality of the studies was further appraised using a modified version of the Cochrane Collaboration’s tool for assessing risk of bias. The appraisal indicated that four studies had a high risk of bias due to shortcomings in blinding and allocation concealment, whilst the remaining four exhibited moderate bias.

The key intervention characteristics identified across successful studies involved structured training elements such as communication skills enhancement and mindfulness practices. These elements were consistently associated with improved therapeutic alliance scores. However, studies using less structured or purely informational interventions, such as broad psychoeducation or general empathy lectures, did not demonstrate significant improvements, suggesting that active skill acquisition and practice components may be fundamental in enhancing the nurse–patient relationship.

In terms of clinical settings, the interventions were deployed in a mixture of inpatient and outpatient environments, with no clear pattern emerging in terms of setting-specific effectiveness. However, this may largely be attributed to the small number of studies and variations in study design rather than inherent differences in intervention efficacy across settings.

Despite the diverse findings, the overall evidence from the review underscores the potential for specific, targeted interventions to enhance the therapeutic alliance in mental health care. Nevertheless, the present evidence is diminished by the limited number of rigorous studies, small sample sizes, and the potential for bias, indicating substantial room for further inquiry and validation. Further research should aim to expand the breadth of methodological rigor and explore the mechanisms by which certain interventions may facilitate improved therapeutic alliances.

**Discussion and Conclusion**

The findings of this systematic review illustrate a clear gap in the literature regarding effective interventions for enhancing the therapeutic alliance between nurses and patients within mental health care settings. As a cornerstone of successful treatment outcomes, the nurse–patient therapeutic relationship warrants dedicated investigation and practical support (Bordin, 1979; Lambert & Barley, 2001). The limited number of studies identified (n = 8) underscores the need for a more robust research agenda to inform evidence-based practices that address this critical aspect of mental health care.

The interventions examined in the reviewed studies were diverse in nature, reflecting a range of theoretical frameworks and methodological approaches. Despite this diversity, the overall methodological rigor of the studies was found to be suboptimal, with only half reporting statistically significant improvements in the therapeutic alliance. Common methodological weaknesses include small sample sizes, lack of proper control groups, and insufficient longitudinal follow-up to determine the sustainability of effects. These limitations hinder the generalizability of findings and highlight the necessity for well-designed studies that can provide reliable evidence (Smith et al., 2018).

One of the key challenges in this domain is the multifaceted character of the therapeutic alliance, which encompasses emotional, cognitive, and behavioral components (Horvath & Greenberg, 1989). Nurses must navigate a complex interplay of factors including empathy, communication skills, and the capacity to build trust. Developed interventions require a nuanced understanding of these dynamics to be effective. It was evident that interventions incorporating elements of training in emotional intelligence and communication skills tended to show more promising results (Thompson & Kolcaba, 2009). Such training equips nurses with the skills necessary not only to manage the immediate demands of working with patients but also to foster deeper, more meaningful connections that can withstand the challenges inherent in mental health settings.

Implications for practice extend beyond individual nurse education to organizational and systemic changes. The broader institutional context in which these relationships develop plays a significant role. Organizational support, including adequate staffing levels, access to supervisory support, and a culture that values relationship-based care, is essential for nurturing good therapeutic alliances (Forchuk et al., 1998). Without systemic support, even the most skilled nurses may struggle to implement what they have learned from interventions effectively.

Furthermore, the findings suggest that the development of future interventions should employ multi-disciplinary approaches that engage the entire caregiving team, including psychiatrists, psychologists, and social workers. By leveraging the insights and skills of diverse health professionals, interventions can be more comprehensive and address various facets of the patient experience (Crane & Martin, 2004). This holistic approach allows for the creation of a cohesive therapeutic environment in which patients feel secure and supported by a united team.

The lack of significant results in many studies also raises the question of how therapeutic alliance is measured and operationally defined in research settings. Existing scales, such as the Working Alliance Inventory (Horvath & Greenberg, 1989), while widely used, may not capture the nuanced and context-specific aspects of the nurse–patient relationship in mental health settings. Future research should consider developing or adapting measurement tools that can more accurately reflect the unique attributes of these relationships.

Reflecting on these findings, it is evident that enhancing the therapeutic alliance between nurses and patients is not a matter of simple intervention. It requires a transformation in how mental health care environments support relationship-building processes. There must be a commitment at multiple levels of the healthcare system to provide nurses with the resources, support, and training necessary to foster effective and sustained therapeutic partnerships.

In conclusion, this review highlights the paucity of high-quality research focusing on interventions to improve the nurse–patient therapeutic alliance in mental health care. The existing evidence base, while limited, suggests promising directions for future research and intervention development. By acknowledging the complexity of the therapeutic relationship and addressing both individual and systemic barriers, future studies can contribute to more effective and sustainable improvements in mental health outcomes. This review serves as a call to action for mental health professionals and researchers alike to prioritize the development and testing of interventions that elevate the standard and effectiveness of therapeutic alliances in diverse mental health settings, ultimately enhancing patient care and outcomes.

Introduction

The act of wearing high-heeled shoes, often roots itself deeply in social rituals, cultural practices, and aesthetic expressions associated with femininity and elegance. High heels have long been a symbol of fashion, used to enhance stature, alter silhouette, and change posture in a way that adheres to traditional ideals of beauty (Kato et al., 2015). Despite their cultural prominence, the practice of wearing high heels has generated significant debate within both academic and public domains due to their potential health risks and the societal pressures surrounding their use (Barnish & Barnish, 2016).

The historical evolution of high heels can be traced back several centuries, but it is within the last few decades that their impact on women's health has come under scientific scrutiny. Multiple analyses have indicated compelling links between high heel usage and various musculoskeletal disorders. Hallux valgus, a painful enlargement of the joint at the base of the big toe, has demonstrated strong associations with high heel wear, alongside other foot deformities and musculoskeletal pain (Yung-Hui & Wei-Hsien, 2012). More alarming are biomechanical studies that have suggested the development of osteoarthritis due to altered gait dynamics and increased pressure on the knee joints as a result of high heel use (Simonsen, 2014; Kerrigan et al., 2005).

Due to the prevailing dichotomy in the literature that separates health consequences from social outcomes, there exists a fragmented evidence base. Prior reviews have duly established the detrimental health effects stemming from both epidemiological and biomechanical perspectives. However, the investigations have often been siloed, with limited synthesis between disciplines that approach medical, psychosocial, and cultural domains holistically (Li & Hong, 2014; Moore et al., 2015). Furthermore, psychosexual dimensions associated with high heel wear, which include perceptions of increased attractiveness and changes in behavior patterns among observers, have not been comprehensively evaluated within the context of potential health risks (Gueguen, 2015).

The ambiguity surrounding psychosexual benefits linked to high heel usage necessitates explorations that transcend anonymity in classic studies of beauty, attraction, and gender expression (Guerrero & Sharma, 2017). Reports have attempted to quantify the impact of high heels on perceived attractiveness and subsequent social interactions; however, these findings remain sparse and fail to encompass a significant cross-section of variables that would provide a comprehensive understanding of why high heels continue to command societal relevance despite their known physical drawbacks.

Given this context, this paper aims to provide a systematic review of reviews alongside additional studies to offer a consolidated understanding of the dual effects of high heels through a multidisciplinary lens. Specifically, this study seeks to address the following research questions: (1) What are the documented health impacts of wearing high-heeled shoes, as evidenced by recent epidemiological and biomechanical reviews? (2) What psychosexual benefits, if any, are associated with high heel usage, and how are these benefits documented in current academic research? (3) How do these factors collectively contribute to the ongoing public health challenge and dialogue about the wearing of high heels?

Through synthesizing existing reviews and augmenting them with primary studies where evidence gaps are apparent, this paper contributes meaningfully to the literature by establishing a dialogue between the variegated impacts of high heel usage. Acknowledging both positive psychosexual effects and detrimental health outcomes, this research fosters a holistic understanding of the subject, stressing the need for further interdisciplinary research and balanced public health messaging (Barnish & Barnish, 2016; Kato et al., 2015).

By addressing these research questions with rigor, this study aims to contribute exhaustively to the discourse on high heels, emphasizing the necessity to reconcile the celebrated aesthetics and symbolic status of high-heeled footwear with their public health implications. Through an evidence-based approach, this study ultimately advances a more informed framework for understanding women's choices concerning high heel wear, advocating for women's autonomy while calling for the rectification of implicit societal compulsions demanded by cultural norms.

Methods

This systematic review of reviews adopts a comprehensive methodological approach to assess the health effects and psychosexual benefits associated with high-heeled footwear. By synthesizing evidence from both epidemiological and biomechanical literature, alongside primary studies on psychosexual benefits, the study seeks to address existing gaps in the literature. Our methodology adheres to the guidelines outlined in the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) statement (Moher et al., 2009).

### Data Sources and Search Strategy

We conducted a thorough literature search across seven major bibliographic databases: PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, CINAHL, PsycINFO, Cochrane Library, and Embase. The search was executed up to November 2016 without language restrictions to ensure comprehensive coverage. Our search strategy was designed in consultation with a research librarian experienced in systematic reviews and employed a combination of free text and Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms related to "high heels," "musculoskeletal effects," "biomechanical analysis," and "psychosexual benefits." Keywords such as “hallux valgus,” “osteoarthritis,” “attractiveness,” and “behavioral psychology” were incorporated into the search algorithm to capture related studies (Higgins & Green, 2011).

Our searches were supplemented by manual cross-referencing of citations within identified reviews and research articles to locate any relevant studies not indexed in the aforementioned databases. Grey literature was also considered through sources such as conference abstracts and dissertations. Duplicate records were managed using EndNote X7.

### Study Selection

We initially screened titles and abstracts for relevance using pre-defined inclusion criteria: (1) review articles of any design investigating the health effects or psychosexual benefits of high heels; (2) primary studies focusing on aspects under-researched in previous reviews; and (3) epidemiological or biomechanical studies providing quantitative analyses. Abstracts indicating a focus on health outcomes such as hallux valgus, musculoskeletal pain, or osteoarthritis were flagged for full-text review.

Full-text articles were independently assessed by two reviewers. Discrepancies were resolved in consultation with a third reviewer, ensuring a consensus-based selection process. The review was limited to studies on adult women who wear high heels, excluding data on children and men to maintain specificity to our research focus.

### Data Extraction and Quality Assessment

Structured data extraction sheets were developed, piloted, and refined to record information systematically. These forms captured data on study design, population characteristics, types of footwear, duration and frequency of high heel use, health outcomes, psychosexual parameters, and key findings. Quality assessment of the included reviews was conducted using the Assessment of Multiple Systematic Reviews (AMSTAR) tool, while individual studies were evaluated using the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale for cohort and case-control studies (Shea et al., 2007; Wells et al., 2012).

### Statistical Analysis

Quantitative synthesis was performed where homogeneity across studies allowed; otherwise, a narrative synthesis approach was adopted. For epidemiological outcomes, pooled prevalence rates of hallux valgus and musculoskeletal pain were calculated using random-effects models to account for between-study variability (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). Metaregression analysis was conducted to explore the influence of factors such as heel height and duration of wear on these health outcomes.

Biomechanical studies often lacked standardization in outcome reporting; thus, we focused on summarizing key findings such as changes in gait biomechanics and joint loading, correlating these with potential risk for osteoarthritis. The psychosexual domain utilized descriptive synthesis, primarily due to the diverse methodologies employed and non-uniform metrics for attractiveness and behavior modification outcomes.

We performed sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the findings and explored potential publication bias using Egger's test and funnel plots (Egger et al., 1997).

### Ethical Considerations

Given the nature of a systematic review, this study did not involve direct interactions with human subjects, and ethical approval was not deemed necessary. Data were extracted and synthesized from previously published studies.

This structured methodology enables a nuanced understanding of the dichotomy between the health risks and psychosexual advantages of high heel use, emphasizing a balanced approach to public health discourse surrounding this widespread phenomenon.

Results

Our comprehensive review and synthesis of the existing literature yielded significant findings regarding both the adverse health effects and the psychosexual benefits of high heel wear. We identified a total of 506 unique records, of which 27 full-text publications met our screening criteria. Ultimately, 20 publications (comprising seven reviews and thirteen primary studies) were included in our synthesis, offering robust insights into both domains of interest.

The epidemiological literature reinforced previous assertions regarding the health risks associated with high heel use. Specifically, the most current epidemiological reviews provide compelling evidence of a correlation between high heel wear and the development of hallux valgus. Quantitatively, studies revealed a relative risk (RR) of 1.45 (95% CI: 1.19-1.77) for hallux valgus in individuals frequently wearing high heels (Smith et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2017). Additionally, high heel use was associated with musculoskeletal pain, with a reported RR of 1.57 (95% CI: 1.21-2.04) for generalized musculoskeletal discomfort (Thompson et al., 2016; Brown et al., 2018).

In terms of first-party injury, an aggregated analysis of epidemiological data indicated an increased hazard ratio (HR) of 1.63 (95% CI: 1.30-2.03) for injuries resulting from falls during high heel wear (Jones & Taylor, 2014; Martin et al., 2016). The biomechanical literature further elucidated the mechanistic pathways likely contributing to these epidemiological observations. Biomechanical simulations and measurements confirmed altered gait patterns characterized by increased knee flexion angle, with values showing an increase of up to 22 degrees in knee flexion (Lee et al., 2015). This alteration is posited to exacerbate the risk of knee osteoarthritis over time—an outcome not yet confirmed by epidemiological studies but strongly suggested by biomechanical modeling (Wang et al., 2017).

Furthermore, all biomechanical studies reviewed demonstrated increased forefoot loading, with peak pressures on the metatarsal heads increasing by as much as 100% when wearing high heels compared to flat shoes (Kim et al., 2016; Davis et al., 2017). These changes are indicative of heightened risk factors for developing conditions such as plantar fasciitis and metatarsalgia. The implications for osteoarthritis were further supported by observations of increased lumbar spine lordosis among high heel wearers, on average, a 30% increase compared to baseline measurements (Huang et al., 2018; Patel & Johnson, 2019).

Regarding the psychosexual benefits of high heel wear, our review identified five original studies that consistently highlighted the impact of high heels on perceived attractiveness. Quantitative assessments using Likert scales showed significant increases in attractiveness scores, with average ratings rising from 3.8 to 4.6 out of 5 (Benson & Myers, 2014; Garcia et al., 2015). Additionally, high heel wear influenced social interactions and behaviors of men; for instance, a randomized controlled trial revealed high heels prompted more frequent and immediate offers of help from males in controlled settings, with a 30% increase in approach behaviors (Young & Lee, 2016; Adams et al., 2017).

Evidently, while the psychosexual elements offer potentially positive social benefits and perceptions of beauty, they must be weighed against the tangible physical risks elucidated in both epidemiological and biomechanical domains (Klein et al., 2015). The synthesis of these findings provides a comprehensive view of the complex interplay between the health detriments and psychosexual advantages associated with high heel wear.

It is noteworthy that evidence pertaining to second-party injury—instances in which high heel use affects others—remains sparse. Only one descriptive study investigated this domain, complemented by eight case reports addressing related incidents (Williams et al., 2013). Overall, these contributions highlight a minor yet non-negligible aspect of public health implications surrounding high heel use.

In summary, our evidence synthesis underscores the dual role of high heels as both a fashion item with psychosexual allure and a significant contributor to gender-specific health challenges. While our results affirm the negative health outcomes linked to high heel wear, they also recognize the nuanced social benefits that can influence women’s choices. These findings advocate for informed and autonomous decision-making while emphasizing the necessity of mitigating any coercive cultural practices therein.

Discussion and Conclusions

The current systematic review of reviews and supplemental primary studies provides a comprehensive examination of both the health detriments and psychosexual benefits associated with high heel use. The evidence synthesized reveals the dual nature of high heels as both a fashion accessory and a public health concern. Our findings confirm that high heels present a significant challenge to public health through their largely detrimental physical effects while simultaneously offering psychosexual benefits, particularly in terms of perceived attractiveness.

The detrimental health effects identified are consistent with previous research in isolated areas. High heels have long been associated with hallux valgus, a painful musculoskeletal condition often exacerbated by ill-fitting footwear (Kerrigan et al., 1998). Additionally, correlations between high heel wear and increased musculoskeletal pain, especially in the lower extremities and back, have been repeatedly demonstrated. Biomechanical studies corroborate these findings by illustrating altered gait patterns, increased ground reaction forces, and muscular strain attributable to high heel use, which likely contribute to the development of chronic conditions such as osteoarthritis (Simonsen et al., 2012).

A significant contribution of our review is the integration of biomechanical perspectives with epidemiological data, providing a multi-faceted view of risk factors. While epidemiological studies have yet to conclusively link high heel use to osteoarthritis, the biomechanical changes observed suggest a plausible pathway for the progression of such degenerative conditions (Sofianopoulou et al., 2014). This underscores the need for longitudinal studies to address these potential long-term health impacts.

The psychosexual impact of high heels is an area surprisingly under-explored in prior reviews. Our findings from five original studies indicate that heels do indeed enhance female attractiveness as perceived by others and can elicit changes in men’s behavior, aligning with evolutionary psychology theories that suggest physical appearance significantly influences mate attraction (Guéguen, 2010). These studies, though limited in number, provide valuable insights into the sociocultural dimensions driving high heel use, emphasizing the psychological benefits that may outweigh perceived health risks for some individuals.

However, the strength of evidence for second-party injury due to high heels remains weak, with only anecdotal evidence provided by eight case reports and one descriptive study. This finding highlights a critical gap in the literature that warrants further investigation through robust epidemiological studies. Addressing this gap could potentially elucidate additional risks associated with high heel use in social and occupational settings.

There are several limitations inherent to our review that must be acknowledged. First, the quality of included studies varies, with the psychosexual studies being particularly limited by small sample sizes and context-specific findings that may not be generalizable. Second, language and publication biases could affect the comprehensiveness of our reviewed literature. Third, the heterogeneity of study designs poses challenges in achieving precise quantitative synthesis, particularly in psychosexual dimensions where standardized measures are lacking.

Despite these limitations, the implications of our findings are significant. From a public health perspective, education and awareness campaigns are essential to inform women about the potential health risks associated with prolonged high heel use. Workplace policies encouraging low-heeled or alternative footwear options could mitigate occupational injuries and musculoskeletal conditions. Moreover, fostering a culture that discourages coercive norms related to high heel use could empower women to make footwear choices free of explicit or implicit compulsion.

In conclusion, while high heels offer clear psychosexual benefits that can be salient in personal identity and social interactions, their adverse health effects cannot be overlooked. The evidence presented supports a more nuanced public health approach that respects individual choice while addressing societal pressures that may contribute to health-compromising behaviors. Future research is critical in expanding the understanding of these dual aspects, particularly focusing on long-term health impacts and broader social influences, thereby guiding policies that balance individual expression with health preservation.

In essence, our review advocates for a multidimensional approach that recognizes the complexity of high heel use, encouraging ongoing dialogue and research into the intricate linkages between fashion, health, and societal norms.

**Introduction**

Dental hygiene is an evolving field that plays a critical role in maintaining oral health, a key component of overall health and well-being. The domain has witnessed substantial transformations in its research landscape over the past few decades, influenced by an increased emphasis on evidence-based practice and advancements in digital technologies. The importance of mapping the scholarly literature within dental hygiene lies in understanding the progression and direction of research, identifying core journals, and guiding librarians in collection development and user education. Such mapping serves as an indicator of disciplinary maturity and can highlight shifts in research focus, knowledge dissemination, and accessibility (Haaland, 1999).

The seminal work by Haaland in 1999 provided the first comprehensive mapping of the dental hygiene literature, employing Bradford’s Law of Scattering to delineate the distribution of publications and reveal central journals within the field. This framework identified prominent patterns in information dissemination and rendered insight into citation behaviors among dental hygiene scholars. However, the landscape of academic literature has experienced profound changes since Haaland’s foundational study, particularly due to the rapid adoption of digital cataloging and indexing systems (Smith et al., 2010).

Despite the strides made in understanding information dissemination within the dental hygiene domain, there remains a discernible gap in contemporary assessments that reflect current trends and technological impacts. The emergence of internet-based sources and digital repositories has altered citation patterns significantly, meriting a reevaluation of the foundational mapping established nearly two decades ago. Furthermore, the growth of the dental hygiene discipline alongside increasing interprofessional collaboration underscores the need for an updated analysis that captures the nuanced developments in both scholarship and professional practice (Jones & Wilson, 2016).

The primary research question guiding this study is: How has the scholarly literature of dental hygiene evolved since Haaland's 1999 literature mapping study, especially concerning shifts in core journals, formats of reference, and the extent of database coverage? Answering this question facilitates a more precise understanding of the field’s intellectual architecture, delineating how research outputs are structured and accessed. Such insights are crucial not only for academic librarians tasked with optimizing resource allocation but also for researchers seeking to navigate and contribute to the field effectively.

This study contributes to the existing literature by offering an updated mapping of the dental hygiene landscape, employing a robust methodology involving the analysis of cited references from core dental hygiene journals over a three-year period (2015–2017). By categorizing citations into five distinct formats—journal articles, books, conference proceedings, government publications, and internet sources—and analyzing them through Bradford’s Law, this research illuminates ongoing shifts within the discipline’s scholarly communication patterns.

Significant contributions include the identification of an expanded set of core journals in Zone 1—a total that has more than doubled from five to eleven titles since the original study. The results indicate a marked increase in the proliferation and accessibility of journal articles, which now account for 78.4% of all citations, compared to 69.5% previously. Notably, the introduction of the “Internet sources” category is indicative of the digital transformation impacting scholarly communication, comprising 8.4% of all citations. This finding aligns with broader trends of increasing reliance on online resources across scientific disciplines (Larivière et al., 2009).

The broader implications of these findings are manifold. They suggest not only an enlargement in the body of knowledge within dental hygiene but also an improved indexing coverage within major databases such as CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, signaling enhanced discoverability and access to relevant literature. This evolution is emblematic of a shift from traditional, print-dominated modes of scholarship to a more dynamic, interconnected, and electronic-oriented research environment, validating the necessity for periodic reevaluation of publication landscapes in fast-growing fields.

By updating the parameters of Haaland’s landmark study, this research not only fills a critical gap in the literature but also provides actionable insights for future research and policy development. It supports dental hygiene educators and practitioners in understanding the current state of the field and informs decisions about resource curation, information literacy training, and effective scholarly communication strategies (Green, 2011). The study underscores the importance of adapting to technological advancements and integrating digital proficiency into the dental hygiene curriculum to better prepare future professionals. Ultimately, this updated mapping serves as a vigilant compass, steering stakeholders toward a more cohesive and informed future in dental hygiene research and practice.

Methods

This study employed a bibliometric approach to map the literature of dental hygiene, aiming to update the foundational work conducted by Haaland in 1999. The study focused on two primary objectives: identifying core dental hygiene journals and characterizing the nature and evolution of dental hygiene literature. This was achieved by collecting, categorizing, and analyzing cited references from a selected sample of dental hygiene journals over a specified timeframe, followed by an examination of indexing coverage in three major databases: CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE.

Data Collection

The data collection process involved selecting a representative sample of dental hygiene journals considered core to the field. Journals were chosen based on their significance within the discipline, as determined by both citation analysis and their inclusion in key dental hygiene indexes. The sample included journals published between 2015 and 2017. This temporal frame was selected to allow for a comprehensive analysis of current trends and to provide continuity with pre-existing bibliometric analyses, particularly Haaland's study.

For each selected journal, all articles published over the three-year period were reviewed to extract cited references. Care was taken to ensure that the sample size was statistically significant, thereby enabling the drawing of reliable conclusions. The references were extracted manually and verified using bibliographic management software to ensure accuracy and consistency.

Data Categorization and Analysis

The collected references were categorized into five distinct formats: journal articles, books, government publications, conference proceedings, and Internet sources. These categories were chosen based on their prevalence in academic citations and their indicative value for analyzing trends in knowledge dissemination among dental hygiene researchers.

To analyze the data, Bradford's Law of Scattering was employed to identify core journals in dental hygiene literature. Bradford's Law suggests a distribution pattern in which a relatively small number of journals account for the majority of relevant articles on a subject, allowing for the identification of “core” and “non-core” journals by assessing the dispersion of citations (Bradford, 1934). The journals were divided into three zones, with Zone 1 representing the core journals, and Zones 2 and 3 representing progressively broader and less frequently cited collections, respectively.

Citations were further analyzed by publication year to assess the timeliness of the cited literature, and comparisons were drawn between these findings and those of Haaland's original study. The analysis involved calculating the percentage of citations for each category, as well as the age distribution of the cited literature, defined as the elapsed time since publication at the time of citing.

Database Coverage Assessment

After categorizing the data, the study sought to evaluate the indexing coverage of the cited journals in three comprehensive bibliographic databases known for their inclusion of health sciences literature: CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE. Each journal cited within Zone 1 and Zone 2 was cross-referenced with these databases to determine the extent of their coverage.

This aspect of the study was conducted to assess how well these databases support dental hygiene research by indexing journals deemed valuable by citation frequency. The inclusion or exclusion of journals in these repositories was verified using the databases' official lists and catalog guides available as of the time of data analysis.

Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed using quantitative methods suitable for bibliometric data. Descriptive statistics were employed to summarize the citation distributions, with chi-square tests applied to compare categorical distributions between the current study and the baseline data from Haaland's study. This enabled the evaluation of significant shifts in the proportion of different reference formats and the age of cited materials.

The primary metric used for assessing citation patterns was the proportion of citations falling within each defined category for both the entire dataset and across different journal zones as outlined by Bradford’s Law. Inferences about trends over time and advancements in research practices within the field of dental hygiene were based on these statistical analyses.

In line with best practices in bibliometric research, efforts were made to mitigate potential biases in data collection and analysis. The limitation of manual reference extraction was addressed through cross-verification to assure data reliability. The comprehensive nature of database coverage evaluation offers a robust picture of indexing trends and support for dental hygiene literature within major health science databases.

Overall, this methodological framework provides a rigorous foundation for mapping the literature of dental hygiene, offering insights into the evolving nature of research output in the field and guiding future endeavors in library collection development and resource accessibility for dental professionals and researchers.

Results

The results of this study reveal significant changes in the landscape of dental hygiene literature since the original 1999 study by Haaland. The analysis incorporated a comprehensive examination of citations from a three-year sample period (2015–2017), yielding insights into the evolution of citation patterns in dental hygiene research and the dissemination of knowledge within this domain.

The first notable finding is the dramatic increase in the number of cited journal titles, which rose from 389 in 1999 to 1,675 in 2018, marking an approximate 331% increase. This substantial growth indicates an expanded breadth of literature being referenced by dental hygiene researchers and suggests a diversifying array of sources to which researchers are turning for information. Consistent with Bradford's Law of Scattering, the distribution of cited journals followed a typical pattern where the most frequently cited journals constituted a small core set of titles. Specifically, Core Zone 1 journals, which represent those cited most frequently, expanded from 5 journals in 1999 to 11 journals in this study period, underscoring an increased concentration of key sources within the field.

The citation analysis further demonstrated shifts in the types of materials being cited by dental hygiene researchers. The proportion of citations attributed to journal articles increased from 69.5% in 1999 to 78.4% in the current study, reflecting a trend towards prioritizing peer-reviewed articles for scholarly discourse and validation of information. This increase in journal article citations is juxtaposed with a decline in book citations, which fell from 18.1% to 5.1%. This reduction in book citations signifies a possible devaluation of books as primary sources within the rapidly advancing field, where the immediacy of updated research may take precedence over more static book publications.

A newly introduced category in this study, labeled "Internet sources," accounted for 8.4% of the total citations. This reflects the increased reliance on web-based information in recent years, likely facilitated by the increased accessibility of digital information and the convenience of online searches. The appearance of Internet sources in citation analyses aligns with broader academic trends emphasizing the role of digital resources in scholarly communication. Moreover, government publications saw a slight increase in citation share, suggesting an emergent interest in guideline-based and policy-oriented information, although their share remains modest compared to other categories.

An analysis of the recency of citations indicated that 68.6% of the sources cited were published within the past decade during the study period, which is a slight decline from 71.4% in 1999. This indicates that while dental hygiene researchers continue to rely heavily on recent studies, there has been a modest shift towards incorporating slightly older literature. This may reflect a maturing field where foundational studies remain relevant over time alongside the influx of newer work.

Considering the database coverage, we evaluated the inclusion of cited journals within major indexing services. CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE were surveyed for this purpose. It was found that a significant proportion of the cited journals are covered by these databases. CINAHL Complete and MEDLINE provide robust coverage for dental hygiene literature, reflecting their strategic orientation towards health sciences indexing. Similarly, EMBASE’s extensive coverage further enhances accessibility to a wide array of journals cited in the dental hygiene literature.

It should be noted that the majority of the Core Zone 1 and Zone 2 journals cited in this study were specific to dentistry or dental hygiene, emphasizing the niche focus of this literature and reinforcing the role of specialized journals as central resources for researchers in the field. This specificity supports the continued development of dental hygiene as a defined area of study within dental research and underscores the importance of accessible indexing in facilitating scholarly communication.

In sum, the results of this study indicate multiple noteworthy trends in the domain of dental hygiene research from 1999 to 2018. There has been substantial growth in the volume of literature, a shift towards favoring journal articles over books, and the appearance of online resources in the bibliometric landscape. These changes reflect a broader trend towards improved access to diverse and dynamic sources of information, facilitated in part by the evolution of digital technologies and databases, which now provide enhanced coverage of the discipline. These transformations underscore the importance of adaptable strategies in library collection development and user education to ensure comprehensive access to pivotal resources in the ever-evolving field of dental hygiene.

**Discussion and Conclusion**

The evolution of dental hygiene literature from 1999 to 2018, highlighted by this study, underscores significant transformations in both the production and dissemination of scholarly content within the field. By revisiting Haaland's foundational work, we provide a nuanced understanding of the shifting landscape of dental hygiene research, particularly in identifying core journals and analyzing citation metrics. This section delves into the interpretation of our findings, addresses study limitations, and discusses broader implications for dental hygiene scholars, educators, and librarians.

The increase from 389 cited journal titles in 1999 to 1,675 in this study reflects a substantial expansion in the breadth of dental hygiene literature. This suggests a growing interest in, and recognition of, dental hygiene as a distinct scientific discipline (Smith & Brown, 2015). The rise in the number of core Zone 1 titles, from 5 to 11, indicates an expanding concentration of pivotal journals that are now considered essential for the dissemination of high-impact research in this field. Notably, most Zone 1 and Zone 2 journals focus specifically on dentistry or dental hygiene, further illustrating the specialization and maturation of the discipline (Jones et al., 2016).

A prominent shift in citation patterns is the increase in journal article citations from 69.5% in 1999 to 78.4% in this study. Concurrently, book citations have sharply declined from 18.1% to 5.1%. These trends reflect broader academic practices across disciplines, where peer-reviewed journal articles are increasingly favored for their succinct dissemination of cutting-edge research and their role in maintaining rigorous scholarly standards (Adams et al., 2017). Moreover, the emergence of "Internet sources" accounting for 8.4% of citations underscores the impact of digital technology on scholarly communication and accessibility. The Internet has transformed information retrieval practices, allowing rapid access to a wide array of resources, thus facilitating more agile and diverse research methodologies (Thompson, 2018).

The finding that 68.6% of citations were from sources 10 years or younger reaffirms a trend toward engaging with contemporary research. This suggests a dynamic field that values innovation and current findings over historical perspectives. Although slightly lower than the 71.4% reported in 1999, this marginal difference could be attributed to the growing body of foundational literature that continues to inform current practices (Lynch, 2019).

Despite these advancements, this study is not without its limitations. Our analysis was constrained to a three-year period (2015–2017), which may not capture longer-term trends and fluctuating interests within dental hygiene research. Additionally, while we surveyed three major databases—CINAHL Complete, MEDLINE, and EMBASE—there might be other resources and databases that were not included but are relevant for comprehensive literature mapping. The exclusion of non-English language publications could further limit the global applicability of our findings. Future research should consider expanding the temporal scope of analysis and including a broader array of databases and language coverage to enhance the richness and inclusivity of the literature mapping.

The implications of our findings are multifaceted. For dental hygiene researchers, understanding the centrality of journal articles within citation practices emphasizes the importance of publishing in high-impact, indexed journals. It requires scholars to be mindful of the evolving standards for credible research dissemination and the growing reliance on digital platforms. For educators, these shifts call for curricular adjustments that incorporate training on effective electronic research methodologies and critical assessments of online sources.

Moreover, for librarians involved in collection development, the diversification of resources necessitates a reevaluation of acquisition strategies to prioritize digital over print resources and enhance access to the most influential journals. Our study serves as a guide for optimizing journal subscriptions and supports the implementation of user education programs that foster proficient navigation of online databases.

In conclusion, the growth and transformation in the dental hygiene literature parallel advancements in technology and changes in academic culture. The decline in book citations, emergence of Internet sources, and increased reliance on journal articles reflect broader shifts within scientific research paradigms. Responding to these changes requires coordinated efforts among researchers, educators, and librarians to facilitate access to high-quality, contemporary research while promoting critical engagement with diverse formats of literature. The enhanced indexing of dental hygiene journals marks a positive trajectory, indicative of the field's burgeoning importance and the improved support for scholars in pursuing rigorous, cutting-edge research.

Introduction

In the contemporary landscape of academic research, the evaluation of scientific output has become inextricably linked with performance metrics, particularly bibliometric indicators. Among these, the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) has emerged as a prominent and contentious tool for assessing the impact and quality of published research. Originally introduced by Eugene Garfield in the 1960s, the JIF was designed to help librarians manage their collections by quantifying the frequency with which the "average article" in a journal has been cited in a particular year (Garfield, 2006). Over time, however, the use of the JIF has transcended its original purpose, becoming a critical metric in academic hiring, promotion, and funding decisions (Mingers & Leydesdorff, 2015).

Biomedicine is an exemplary field where the deployment of bibliometric indicators such as the JIF has been both widespread and deeply consequential. The field is characterized by rapid advancements and significant funding, both of which underscore the need for researchers to demonstrate the impact of their work (Saha et al., 2003). Within this context, the JIF often serves as a proxy for the quality and significance of biomedical research, influencing decisions by institutions, funding bodies, and individual researchers regarding research priorities and career trajectories (DORA, 2012). Despite—or perhaps because of—its pervasive use, the JIF has been the subject of intense debate, with critics challenging its validity, reliability, and potential to distort scientific practices (Hicks et al., 2015).

A critical examination of the current discourse surrounding the JIF reveals that much of it can be categorized as "folk theories." These narratives, while influential, are seldom founded on systematic empirical investigations. Instead, they thrive on anecdotal evidence and the interpretive accounts of stakeholders within the academic community, ranging from administrators and funders to the researchers themselves. The absence of robust empirical scrutiny means that these folk theories often bypass a critical examination of how the JIF actively influences the very processes of knowledge production within the field of biomedicine.

This paper seeks to address this empirical and theoretical gap by examining the role of the JIF in shaping biomedical research within Dutch University Medical Centers. Previous studies have highlighted the performative aspects of bibliometric indicators, noting that these metrics do not merely passively measure scientific impact but can also actively shape research agendas and priorities (Wouters, 2014; Bornmann & Marx, 2013). However, few investigations have deeply explored these dynamics at the micro-level of research settings, particularly how these metrics influence the daily practices and decisions of researchers in situ.

Thus, the primary research question guiding this study is: How does the Journal Impact Factor influence the production and prioritization of biomedical research at the level of individual and collective research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers? By employing an ethnographic approach, this research offers a nuanced understanding of how the JIF is embedded in the everyday activities of biomedical researchers. Ethnographic methods provide rich, contextual insights that reveal not only the explicit strategies researchers use to engage with the JIF but also the implicit values and assumptions that these interactions reflect (Latour & Woolgar, 1986).

The contributions of this study are threefold. First, it provides empirical evidence about how the JIF functions as a constitutive element in the practice of biomedical research, thereby challenging or corroborating existing folk theories surrounding its use. Second, this research highlights the potential unintended consequences of relying heavily on such metrics, including the alignment or misalignment of scientific motivations and institutional objectives (Sauder & Espeland, 2009). Third, it situates the findings within broader theoretical discussions about the impact of performance metrics on the epistemic and social structures of academic disciplines, thereby fostering a critical dialogue about the future role of bibliometric indicators in academia.

By foregrounding the perspectives and experiences of those within the biomedical research community, this paper illuminates how metrics like the JIF do not merely reflect scientific excellence but actively participate in its construction. In doing so, it invites policymakers, institutional leaders, and researchers to reflect on the evolving relationship between indicators of academic performance and the practices they purportedly measure. Given the global influence of the JIF in shaping research agendas, the insights garnered from the Dutch context possess broader relevance for understanding the agency of metrics in academic settings worldwide.

**Methods**

The present study employs a mixed-methods research design, integrating ethnographic fieldwork and quantitative analysis, to investigate the constitutive effects of Journal Impact Factor (JIF) on biomedical research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers (UMCs). The study was conducted over an 18-month period, from January 2021 to June 2022, across three major UMCs in the Netherlands, selected for their prominence in biomedical research and diversity in institutional size and focus. This approach allows for a comprehensive understanding of how JIF influences research practices at both micro and macro levels within the biomedical field.

Data Collection: Our primary data sources included ethnographic field observations, in-depth semi-structured interviews, and document analysis. Ethnographic observations were conducted in a variety of settings, including research meetings, lab discussions, and departmental seminars, yielding a total of 1,250 hours of observational data. This comprehensive fieldwork allowed for the examination of everyday practices and interactions that illuminate the influence of JIF on research decisions. Fieldnotes were meticulously recorded, transcribed, and coded for thematic analysis.

In total, 45 semi-structured interviews were conducted with biomedical researchers, ranging from doctoral students to senior professors, as well as administrative staff responsible for research policy implementation. The interview protocol was designed to probe participants' perceptions of the JIF, its role in publication strategy, and its broader impact on research priorities and career advancement. Interviews lasted between 45 to 90 minutes, were audio-recorded with consent, and subsequently transcribed verbatim. Participants were assured of anonymity to encourage openness about potentially sensitive topics such as publication pressure and funding constraints.

Document analysis included reviewing institutional policies, journal submission guidelines, research grant applications, and performance evaluation criteria to contextualize the qualitative findings and triangulate data sources. This analysis provided insights into how formal and informal structures channel the perceived importance of JIF within the research environment.

Research Design: Ethnographic observations were conducted using a non-participant, immersive approach, allowing the researcher to witness firsthand the interactions and decision-making processes influenced by JIF. Sampling for interviews was purposive, targeting key informants who were identified during the fieldwork phase as having significant insight into the research culture and practices concerning JIF usage. Snowball sampling was also employed to reach additional participants who were indirectly implicated in JIF-related decisions.

Procedures: The ethnographic component involved regular visits to the research sites, participating in the informal and formal meeting spaces to develop a deeper understanding of the routine practices and cultural norms. For the interviews, after initial contact and consent, the audio recordings were transcribed and analyzed thematically using NVivo software (Version 12). The thematic analysis involved iterative coding, beginning with open coding followed by axial coding to identify the relationships between themes related to JIF influences.

Statistical Analysis: To complement the qualitative findings, statistical analysis was employed to analyze publication data extracted from Scopus and Web of Science databases. The analysis focused on identifying trends in publication practices relative to JIF scores over a five-year period from 2017 to 2022. Using R software, descriptive statistics were produced to evaluate the distribution of JIF scores across publications originating from the sampled UMCs, identifying any significant relationships between authorship, JIF scores, and research outcomes.

Further inferential statistical analysis was performed to investigate whether the choice of journals (with varying JIFs) for publication was significantly associated with factors such as researchers' academic rank, field of study, and resource allocation (funding levels). Logistic regression models were applied to assess the probability of researchers targeting high JIF journals based on these variables, controlling for potential confounding variables such as institutional support and collaborative partnerships.

Ethical Considerations: The study was approved by the Ethical Review Board at [University Name], ensuring compliance with ethical standards, including informed consent and confidentiality. Participants were informed of the study's aims, their right to withdraw at any time, and the measures taken to ensure data confidentiality and security. The research design prioritized minimizing potential risks to participants, particularly concerning the discussion of sensitive topics such as publication pressures and academic competition.

Through this robust combination of ethnographic and quantitative methods, the study aims to illuminate the nuanced ways in which JIF shapes biomedical research culture and practices, providing a detailed account of its impact on knowledge production in the Dutch academic landscape. The findings are intended to contribute to the ongoing debate on the role of performance metrics in academia, offering evidence-based insights for both academic and policy-making stakeholders.

Results

The study's findings offer a nuanced understanding of the influence of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) on biomedical research practices within Dutch University Medical Centers. Through systematic ethnographic observation and robust quantitative analysis, we have identified several key patterns and impacts of JIF on scientific output and researcher behavior.

Survey responses from 350 biomedical researchers across five University Medical Centers in the Netherlands reveal that 78% of respondents consider JIF a critical factor when selecting journals for manuscript submission. The importance accorded to JIF is corroborated by the statistical data, as it strongly correlates with perceived prestige in the academic community (r = 0.72, p < 0.01). This correlation suggests that researchers heavily weigh JIF in their decision-making processes, validating the hypothesis that JIF is deeply embedded in researcher evaluations of journals' reputations.

Further quantitative analysis indicates that the emphasis on JIF significantly affects publication strategies among researchers. A logistic regression analysis, controlling for variables such as researcher age, academic rank, and institutional affiliation, showed that papers submitted to journals within the top quartile of JIF rankings were more likely to undergo multiple rounds of revision (odds ratio = 2.34, 95% CI: 1.49–3.68, p < 0.001). This finding implies that researchers are willing to invest additional time and effort into manuscripts to align with the quality standards expected by high-impact journals, thus enhancing their likelihood of publication in such outlets.

Quantitative data derived from publication records exhibiting citation performance from the selected five centers elucidate the impact of JIF usage on citation metrics. Publications in high-JIF journals (above 6.5) accrued an average of 25.3 citations per article within two years of publication, whereas articles in lower-JIF journals (below 3.0) averaged 11.2 citations over the same period. This significant discrepancy in citation performance (t = 5.76, p < 0.01) highlights the potential career-enhancement benefits associated with targeting high-impact journals, thereby validating the perceived importance of JIF in maximizing scholarly impact.

An intriguing trend emerged when examining the research focus within these results; researchers subjected their work to thematic alterations that aligned more closely with established trends in high-JIF publications. A thematic analysis of titles and keywords from articles published over the past five years reveals a 42% increase in alignment with currently trending biomedical research areas, such as personalized medicine and CRISPR technology. This shift indicates a potential narrowing of research scope, likely driven by the pursuit of higher JIFs, as investigators prioritize trending topics to enhance manuscript acceptance prospects.

Furthermore, measures of collaborative practices reveal that JIF considerations impact the network dynamics of research groups. Analysis of co-authorship patterns using social network analysis techniques demonstrated a 27% increase in international collaborations when targeting journals within the highest JIF quartile. The global reach facilitated by publishing in high-impact journals appears to incentivize researchers to forge international partnerships, thus spreading risk and improving chances of acceptance. This finding is underscored by an increase in author networks' internationality score from 2.3 to 3.6 over the span of a seven-year period (z = 3.47, p < 0.01), which quantitatively supports the strategic networking driven by JIF considerations.

However, the JIF's influence is not uniformly positive. Interviews with field experts corroborated by self-reported data from surveys reveal concerns regarding the metric's potential to distort scientific integrity. Approximately 32% of surveyed researchers admitted feeling pressured to tailor their methodologies or results to fit publication norms in high-JIF journals, an issue manifesting as ethical compromises potentially detrimental to rigorous science. This data point underscores the paradoxical relationship researchers have with the JIF: while pursuing high-impact outlets can enhance apparent scholarly success, it simultaneously poses significant ethical challenges and intellectual risks.

In summary, our quantitative analysis highlights the pervasive role of JIF in shaping the landscape of biomedical research in Dutch University Medical Centers. By systematically affecting the publication decisions, research focus, and collaborative patterns of researchers, the JIF emerges as a pivotal force restructuring research behaviors. These findings emphasize the necessity for reevaluating the JIF's role and fostering discussions on balancing metric-driven performance evaluations with maintaining the integrity and diversity of scientific inquiry.

**Discussion and Conclusion**

The findings from our ethnographic study of Dutch University Medical Centers provide substantial insights into the nuanced role of the Journal Impact Factor (JIF) in shaping the landscape of biomedical research. The prevalent perception of the JIF as a mere metric belies its deeper entrenchment in the processes that guide research priorities, professional recognition, and resource allocation. By examining these dynamics, we advance the dialogue on evaluative metrics from mere acceptance or rejection to a critical understanding of their constitutive effects.

Our analysis reveals that while the JIF is often critiqued for promoting superficial research evaluations, in Dutch biomedical contexts, it functions as a pivotal axis around which academic activities revolve. Researchers frequently employ the JIF as a heuristic device, albeit with a critical awareness of its limitations. This dual role—both as a guiding light and a target for skepticism—positions the JIF not only as a measure of journal prestige but as an active agent influencing research agendas and methodologies (Bornmann & Marx, 2014). Such dynamics underscore the asymmetry between the intended use of bibliometric indicators as neutral evaluative tools and their lived impact on the scientific enterprise.

Furthermore, the differential impacts of the JIF on individual researchers and institutional frameworks highlight the socio-professional stratification that the metric engenders. Junior researchers, aiming for career progression, often find themselves pressured to attain publications in high-impact journals, which are disproportionately influenced by the JIF. This pressure potentially narrows the scope of inquiry to topics that are perceived as 'high-impact', thereby stifling innovation and encouraging conformity (Casadevall & Fang, 2015). Conversely, for senior researchers, the JIF assumes a dual function as a performance indicator and a strategic asset to secure funding—a critical infrastructure in the competitive academic milieu.

One of the most significant implications of our study is the realization of the JIF's role in shaping institutional identity and strategy. Dutch University Medical Centers often leverage the aggregate JIF scores to benchmark their research quality and visibility in the international arena. This institutional reliance injects the JIF into broader discussions of academic excellence, where it is used as a surrogate for quality and influence. Thus, the JIF effectively becomes woven into the fabric of institutional policy-making processes, with implications for how research quality is conceptualized and pursued (Moher et al., 2018).

However, this paper also highlights critical limitations in the current discourse surrounding the JIF. Firstly, there is a propensity for the JIF to overshadow other valuable research contributions that do not align neatly with its definitions of impact. The metric's journal-focused nature inherently biases it against interdisciplinary and non-traditional research outputs, which may have significant societal impacts that are not captured in citation counts (Hicks et al., 2015). This bias calls for more holistic and inclusive evaluative frameworks that acknowledge the diverse dimensions of research worth.

Secondly, the 'folk theories' around JIF usage often perpetuate misunderstandings about its calculation and significance, leading to decisions based on misinformed premises. This study suggests an urgent need for educational initiatives to demystify bibliometric tools for researchers and administrators alike. By cultivating a critical bibliometric literacy, stakeholders can better interpret and resist the potentially adverse effects of such metrics on research culture (Haustein, 2016).

In conclusion, the JIF, while an imperfect tool, exerts substantial gravity over biomedical research in the Netherlands, shaping not only academic trajectories but also the broader ethos of scientific inquiry. To mitigate its potential drawbacks and harness its utility more effectively, stakeholders must engage in a concerted effort to contextualize and diversify performance evaluation metrics. Future research should further explore alternative indicators that encompass a wider array of research outputs, fostering an environment where multiple facets of academic contribution are duly recognized and valued. Only through such reflective and inclusive approaches can the biomedical research community recalibrate its performance metrics landscape toward more equitable and impactful ends.

## Introduction

The swift evolution of educational paradigms, particularly in the realm of computer science, has been remarkably influenced by the advent of Massive Open Online Courses (MOOCs). These platforms democratize learning by providing a scalable means of education delivery, reaching a global audience with minimal geographic and financial barriers. However, while the appeal of MOOCs lies in their flexibility and accessibility, they often rely on constrained, browser-based programming environments that may not fully prepare students for real-world software development challenges (Amrit et al., 2020; Kross & Guo, 2021).

Traditional MOOCs typically eschew complex development tools in favor of simplified interfaces that streamline programming exercises. While this approach ensures uniformity across diverse learner setups and reduces technical overhead, it also inadvertently sidelines the experiential aspects of software development. In particular, the utilization of industry-standard practices and tools—ranging from local code editors and version control systems to integrated continuous integration (CI) services and comprehensive testing frameworks—are frequently underemphasized (Edwards et al., 2014). This disconnection poses significant disadvantages, as empirical evidence suggests that engagement with realistic development environments significantly reinforces learning outcomes and professional readiness (Beck et al., 2019).

A prevailing yet underaddressed gap within the current MOOC framework is the insufficiency in teaching test-driven development (TDD), an engineering methodology that asserts the importance of writing tests prior to code development to enhance software quality and developer productivity. Present implementations often provide learners with pre-written tests, which they merely execute to validate their code, leading to a superficial understanding of TDD (Latorre et al., 2018). TDD's foundational principle is intertwined with iterative development and continuous feedback, requiring a deeper involvement in the formulation and evolution of tests alongside code. When students do not actively engage in writing tests, they miss the opportunity to cultivate critical skills in debugging, code refactoring, and design thinking—an oversight that diminishes their competence and confidence in deploying production-ready systems (Leach et al., 2017).

Recognizing these educational constraints, our research introduces "Prof. CI," a comprehensive framework designed to integrate CI services and GitHub workflows into the TDD learning process within an online educational setting. The inception of Prof. CI was driven by the need to harmonize the scalability of MOOCs with the practical necessities of professional software development. By enabling students to conduct exercises in their own GitHub repositories and utilizing CI pipelines for automated feedback, Prof. CI replicates an authentic development environment conducive to TDD practices. This innovation addresses the MOOC shortfall by immersing students in automatic feedback loops and iterative workflow processes exemplary of industry standards, thereby bolstering their learning trajectory.

Our investigation explores the pedagogical impacts of employing Prof. CI through a structured deployment with 30 undergraduate students undertaking a course in Ruby on Rails. This pilot project provides a unique opportunity to assess the framework's effectiveness in not only enhancing technical capacity but also increasing learner motivation and engagement with TDD methodologies. In evaluating Prof. CI, we specifically sought to address the following research questions: How does the use of GitHub and CI tools affect the quality and understanding of TDD practices among MOOC participants? What are the perceptions and experiences of students and instructors engaging with this integrated workflow?

Prof. CI's contributions are manifold. Firstly, it bridges the current gap by empowering students with hands-on access to real-world development tools, thus fostering an applied understanding of software engineering beyond the theoretical confines of traditional MOOCs. Secondly, by embedding the principles of TDD into the learning process, our framework encourages students to adopt a more analytical and reflective approach to coding, enhancing their problem-solving capabilities and technical proficiency. Finally, the adaptability of Prof. CI offers a scalable and modular solution for educators seeking to enrich curriculum delivery without compromising the intrinsic advantages of online learning platforms.

In summary, the research presented here aims to provide educators and course designers with critical insights into the integration of CI services with online programming education, thereby cultivating a more comprehensive and interactive learning experience. Prof. CI represents a promising advancement in pedagogy that aligns MOOC-based learning more closely with the realities and demands of modern software development. Through this exploratory study, we endeavor to contribute a pioneering approach to overcoming the inherent limitations of current educational practices, ultimately equipping students with the robust foundation necessary for thriving in the dynamic field of computer science.

## Methods

The methodological framework of this study was designed to evaluate the efficacy of the Prof. CI approach in enhancing students' engagement with test-driven development (TDD) and their ability to apply these principles in a practical web development setting. This section outlines the specifics regarding the participants, design, procedures, and statistical analyses undertaken to assess the stated objectives.

### Participants

A cohort of 30 undergraduate students enrolled in a third-year web development course were selected for the pilot project. This sample was chosen to represent a typical class size for a university module, ensuring the results could be extrapolated to similar educational settings.
