In synthesizing this multitude of evidence, we aim to provide policymakers and educational practitioners with a more coherent narrative on the relative importance of class size as a factor in educational achievement. Recognizing the substantial resource implications associated with class size adjustments, this review can guide more informed decisions regarding educational investments and interventions (Hanushek, 2003).

Ultimately, the principal contribution of this review lies in its ability to consolidate disparate strands of research into an accessible and analytically rigorous framework, offering insights that are both theoretically meaningful and practically applicable. By advancing our understanding of the complex relationship between class size and student outcomes, this work aspires to facilitate more effective and equitable educational policies globally.

## Methods

### Data Sources and Search Strategy

The data for this systematic review were sourced through extensive searches of electronic bibliographic databases, internet search engines, and manual searching of key educational journals. The search strategy was defined to capture both published and unpublished literature pertaining to the effects of class size on academic achievement, accommodating a broad international scope (Ponce & Lozano, 2014). We executed these searches up to February 2017, ensuring a comprehensive coverage of available studies related to class size and its influence on educational outcomes. In addition, reference lists from primary studies and related systematic reviews were scrutinized to identify any additional studies that met the inclusion criteria (Booth et al., 2012).

### Inclusion and Exclusion Criteria

The primary criterion for inclusion was the examination of the impact of class size reduction in general education settings, focusing on academic achievements in reading and mathematics among children from kindergarten through 12th grade or equivalent. Eligible studies were required to employ either randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or non-randomized studies (NRS) with well-defined control groups. Qualitative studies were excluded to maintain a quantitative synthesis of data (Shadish et al., 2002). Rigorous screening processes were applied, considering factors such as methodological quality, risk of bias, and the provision of sufficient data for effect size calculation.

### Data Extraction

Data extraction involved multiple reviewers to mitigate bias, using a standardized extraction form to capture key elements such as study design, sample size, population characteristics, intervention details, and outcomes measured. Particular attention was given to how class size was operationalized, the settings of the intervention, and the specific achievements assessed (Higgins & Green, 2011). Discrepancies in data extraction were resolved through discussion or consultation with an independent third reviewer.

### Study Design and Populations

The review encompassed 127 studies, representing 148 papers across 55 diverse populations from 41 countries. Of these, 45 studies analyzed data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) project, a notable longitudinal study conducted in the United States focusing on kindergarten to third-grade students (Finn & Achilles, 1990). While the STAR experiment provided significant insights, only four of these STAR-related studies were suitable for the meta-analysis alongside six additional non-STAR studies due to stringent inclusion conditions.

### Statistical Analysis

A meta-analytical approach was employed to synthesize the results using random effects models to accommodate for potential heterogeneity among the included studies (Borenstein et al., 2009). Effect sizes for reading and mathematics were converted into standardized mean differences (SMDs), facilitating comparison across diverse study designs and contexts. The pooled estimates were weighted by inverse variance methods, with 95% confidence intervals computed to assess the precision of the estimates (Cohn & Becker, 2003).

Sensitivity analyses were conducted to examine the robustness of the pooled effect sizes across methodological quality components, including the potential effects of incorporating studies with unclear effect directions and those using class size as a continuous variable. Key adjustments were included to correct for clustering effects inherent in the STAR dataset, adopting an intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of 0.22, while non-STAR data required no such adjustments (Hox, 2010).

### Results Synthesis

All synthesized results were stratified by the end of the treatment period—typically the end of the academic year—to provide clear temporal relationships between class size interventions and educational outcomes (Wykes et al., 2016). Additionally, the synthesis considered variability in class size reductions, ranging from minimal reductions of one student per class to more substantial reductions involving several students, ensuring detailed coverage of intervention intensity (Konstantopoulos & Chun, 2009).

In conclusion, the statistical analysis adhered to rigorous standards, leveraging advanced meta-analytic techniques to integrate findings from a wide array of studies with varying methodologies, ensuring credible and actionable conclusions concerning the impact of class size on academic achievement.

# Results

This systematic review aimed to assess the impact of class size on academic achievement, focusing specifically on reading and mathematics performance. The analysis included 127 studies encompassing 148 papers, with study populations from 41 countries. Ten of these studies were eligible for meta-analysis, including four that utilized data from the Student Teacher Achievement Ratio (STAR) experiment conducted in the United States during the 1980s. 

In the meta-analysis of non-STAR studies, results for reading achievement were somewhat varied. The primary studies yielded effect sizes ranging from -0.08 to 0.14, with a majority being statistically non-significant. The random effects model, however, demonstrated a statistically significant small positive effect, with a weighted standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.11 (95% CI: 0.05 to 0.16). This suggests that, on average, students in smaller classes score higher in reading than those in larger classes, though the magnitude of the effect is limited. 

In contrast, the analysis of mathematics achievement showed an inconsistency in both the direction and magnitude of effect sizes. The primary study effect sizes for mathematics ranged from -0.41 to 0.11, with most outcomes not reaching statistical significance (SMD = -0.03; 95% CI: -0.22 to 0.16). The negative average effect, though statistically non-significant, indicates that reducing class size may not universally benefit or possibly detract from mathematical achievement among students. 

For studies analyzing data from the STAR experiment, all results consistently reported positive effects, statistically significant for both reading and mathematics. Effect sizes for reading ranged from 0.17 to 0.34, while for mathematics they ranged from 0.15 to 0.33. Despite the consistently positive data from the STAR cohorts, these findings did not meaningfully alter the overarching conclusions drawn from the complete dataset, especially given the limited representativeness of the STAR experiment in global educational contexts.

When assessing the robustness of these results, sensitivity analyses showed that incorporating different components of study quality and varying operational definitions of class size did not substantively change the mean effect estimates. Nevertheless, when including data from primary studies with indeterminate effect directions, the statistical significance for reading was lost. Similarly, adjusting continuous variable class size reductions to one-student rather than standardized deviation did not appreciably impact the overall conclusions.

The findings underscore a nuanced relationship between small class sizes and academic outcomes. For reading, the evidence suggests a small, statistically significant benefit of reduced class sizes. Meanwhile, for mathematics, the impact of class size appears negligible at best, with potential for negative effects that warrant further investigation. Specifically, the likelihood that a randomly selected student's score improves in reading given a smaller class size stands at 53%, compared to a mere 49% for mathematics.

Overall, while the STAR studies offer an optimistic view of the potential benefits of smaller class sizes, their applicability across diverse educational environments might be limited. Additionally, the financial implications of reducing class sizes and the potential for variable impacts on different student subgroups imply a need for deeper investigation into where and how investments in education can be most effectively allocated.

Discussion and Conclusion

The current systematic review provides a critical synthesis of the evidence on the effects of class size reduction on academic achievement in primary and secondary education, consolidating findings from 148 reports across 41 countries. Despite the extensive data set, the meta-analysis included only ten studies due to stringent criteria regarding methodological rigor, emphasizing the need for careful interpretation of our findings.

The results indicate a marginal positive effect of reduced class size on reading achievement, with a standardised mean difference (SMD) of 0.11, translating to a 53% probability that a student in a smaller class would outperform a peer in a larger class on a reading test. This effect size is statistically significant yet categorized as small per conventional benchmarks (Cohen, 1988). Conversely, the effect size for mathematics was negative and statistically insignificant (SMD = -0.03), suggesting no substantial advantage to smaller class sizes for this subject. The slight negative trend may imply potential adverse outcomes for some students, though this result lacks statistical conviction and thus should be interpreted with caution.

The STAR experiments, a prominent subset within our dataset, consistently reported positive effects for both reading and maths. However, the generalizability of these findings is restricted due to the unique context of the original study, which may not reflect broader educational environments (Mosteller, 1995). It is important to consider that the educational systems, cultural factors, and teacher practices significantly influence the efficacy of class size reduction (Blatchford et al., 2003; Hattie, 2009). Therefore, it remains challenging to directly extrapolate the results across diverse educational settings.

One critical limitation of this study lies in the variability of the included research designs and the potential biases inherent in non-randomized studies. Although the included studies were assessed for methodological quality, the influence of confounding factors cannot be entirely dismissed. For instance, variables such as teacher effectiveness, classroom resources, and curriculum differences could contribute to the observed results (Nye et al., 2000; Glass & Smith, 1979). Moreover, the majority of the reviewed studies focus on short-term academic outcomes without capturing potential long-term effects of class size changes on student achievement and attitudes towards learning.

Another consideration is the cost implications of reducing class sizes, which can be significant. Given that the observed effects on achievement are small, policymakers must weigh these benefits against the financial and logistical demands of implementing such changes on a large scale. Cost-benefit analyses in educational policy often highlight alternative strategies, such as enhancing teacher quality or adopting technology-assisted instruction, which may provide more substantial returns on investment (Hanushek & Rivkin, 2013; Rivkin et al., 2005).

Furthermore, our findings underscore the necessity for nuanced approaches that consider varying impacts on different student populations. For example, some research suggests that smaller class sizes may be more beneficial for younger students, those from disadvantaged backgrounds, or students with specific educational needs (Finn & Achilles, 1999; Krueger, 2003). Future research should aim to disaggregate effects by subgroup to provide a clearer picture of whom class size reductions benefit most significantly.

The inconclusive results for mathematics demand additional investigation into the specific interactions between class size and subject matter. It is plausible that the nature of mathematics instruction, which potentially benefits from peer discussion and collaborative learning environments, is less sensitive to class size reductions than reading, which might require more individual attention from teachers (Torgerson et al., 2014). Therefore, pedagogical strategies should be tailored to leverage class size dynamics effectively for different subjects (Shapson et al., 1980).

In conclusion, this systematic review synthesizes a comprehensive body of literature, suggesting that while smaller class sizes may offer slight improvements in reading achievement, the effects on mathematics remain negligible. Policymakers should consider these findings in conjunction with the broader context of educational reform and prioritize resource allocation that maximizes overall educational outcomes. The enduring question of class size effects calls for ongoing research using robust experimental designs, exploring long-term impacts and differential effects among diverse student populations, to better inform policy decisions.

Finally, the educational community must maintain an adaptive mindset, recognizing that reforms such as class size reduction are part of a complex educational ecosystem. Strategies should synergize with other interventions aimed at improving instructional quality and leveraging technological advancements to foster academic excellence for all students.

## Introduction

Biochar (BC), a carbon-rich material produced from the pyrolysis of organic biomass under limited oxygen conditions, has gained significant attention in recent years for its potential benefits in agriculture and environmental management. Its application in soils promises improvements in soil fertility, carbon sequestration, and mitigation of climate change impacts (Lehmann & Joseph, 2015). The intricate structure and properties of BC, including high surface area and porosity, confer it the ability to enhance soil physical and chemical properties, elevate nutrient retention, and boost soil microbial activity (Korkealaakso et al., 2016). Despite these benefits, the intricate interactions between BC and the soil nitrogen (N) cycle raise complex issues and considerable debate in the scientific community.

One critical aspect of BC-soil dynamics is its effect on the N cycle, particularly concerning nitrogen transformations such as nitrification, ammonification, and denitrification processes. Studies have suggested that BC amendments can inadvertently stimulate the biotic oxidation of ammonium (NH4+) to nitrate (NO3−) and subsequently to nitrous oxide (N2O), a potent greenhouse gas (Spokas et al., 2012). This stimulation could potentially upset the fragile balance of nitrogen in the soil, reducing nitrogen use efficiency (NUE) and contributing to environmental nitrogen losses as both NO3− leaching and increased N2O emissions (Schmidt et al., 2014).

Nitrification inhibitors (NIs), such as 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate (DMPP), have been proposed as a mitigation strategy to manage these biotic transformations and their deleterious effects (Zerulla et al., 2001). DMPP functions by hindering the activity of ammonia-oxidizing bacteria and archaea, thereby delaying the conversion of NH4+ to NO3−. While the potential of DMPP to enhance N retention and reduce N2O emissions in non-amended soils is well-documented, its effectiveness in BC-amended soils remains less explored. The intrinsic properties of BC, such as its feedstock source and pyrolysis temperature, likely influence DMPP's behavior in soil matrices, partly through sorption processes (Clough & Condron, 2010).

Sorption, defined as the partitioning of a chemical compound between the liquid and solid phases (Karapanagioti et al., 2014), is a fundamental mechanism that determines the bioavailability and mobility of NIs like DMPP. Enhanced sorption of DMPP on BC can potentially alter its inhibitory effectiveness and longevity in soils, thus influencing the overall nitrogen cycle and its environmental footprint. Despite its importance, the influence of BC characteistics on the sorption dynamics of NIs has received limited empirical investigation, resulting in a significant gap in the current understanding of BC's role in soil nitrogen management.

In addressing this research gap, our study investigates the sorption behavior of DMPP in a range of BC-soil mixtures, with a specific focus on the impact of BC feedstock type and pyrolysis temperature on sorption capacity. The inclusion of different BC types, categorized by their feedstock origin and pyrolysis conditions, allows us to systematically evaluate how these factors influence DMPP sorption. The sorption of DMPP on aged soil-BC mixtures (aged for 15 months) provides further insights into the temporal dynamics of BC-NI interactions, potentially informing long-term agricultural and environmental management practices.

We aim to answer the primary research question: How do different types of biochar, defined by their feedstock and pyrolysis temperature, affect the sorption of the nitrification inhibitor 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate in aged soil-biochar mixtures? This research contributes to the understanding of nitrogen management in BC-amended soils by elucidating the mechanisms governing DMPP sorption, which could ultimately guide the optimization of agronomic practices that utilize BC for soil fertility improvement and environmental conservation.

Through this study, we contribute to the field by providing a comprehensive examination of how various BC characteristics shape the environmental and functional behavior of a widely used nitrification inhibitor. The outcomes of this research can inform BC application guidelines that account for specific soil-NI interactions, potentially maximizing the agronomic benefits of BC while mitigating its risks associated with N2O emissions and nutrient leaching. Our findings also underscore the need for a nuanced approach to BC utilization in agriculture, one that carefully considers the physicochemical interplay between BC, NIs, and soil properties.

Methods

This study was designed to investigate the sorption behavior of the nitrification inhibitor 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate (DMPP) in biochar-amended soils, assessing how biochar (BC) properties influence DMPP interaction within 15-month-aged soil-BC mixtures. The experiment employed a controlled laboratory setup to ensure the reliability and replicability of data gathered across different treatments. 

Soil and Biochar Selection:
The soil utilized in this study originated from an agricultural site characterized as sandy loam with a pH of 6.5, organic carbon content of 1.8%, and cation exchange capacity of 16 cmol/kg. This substrate was chosen for its prevalence in conventional crop-production systems. Four distinct BC types were produced from different feedstocks: hardwood, softwood, straw, and manure. Each feedstock was pyrolyzed at two temperatures—350°C and 600°C—to produce BCs with varying physicochemical properties. These temperatures were selected based on prior studies indicating significant changes in BC structure and functionality across these pyrolysis conditions (Lehmann and Joseph, 2015).

Experimental Design:
Aged BC-soil mixtures were prepared via amendments of soil with 5% (w/w) BC. The mixtures were incubated for 15 months under controlled conditions (25°C, 60% field capacity moisture level) to simulate realistic aging processes. DMPP was employed at a standard agricultural dose of 20 mg/kg soil, applying it uniformly across treatments.

Sorption Experiments:
Batch sorption experiments determined the retention of DMPP in BC-amended soils. Equilibrium studies involved mixing 10 g of BC-soil mixtures with 40 ml of DMPP solution (20 mg/L concentration) in sealed Erlenmeyer flasks. The flasks were placed in an orbital shaker at 120 rpm and 25°C for 48 hours—a duration confirmed sufficient by preliminary kinetic studies (Chen et al., 2017). After equilibration, the suspension was centrifuged at 4,000 rpm for 10 minutes, and the supernatant was analyzed for DMPP concentrations using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) with UV detection at 285 nm.

Data Collection:
Data were collected for DMPP concentration in supernatants, BC inferential impacts on soil hydrophobicity, and soil organic matter content using established methodologies. HPLC parameters were calibrated via standards of known DMPP concentrations, ensuring accuracy within a detection range of 0.1 mg/L to 100 mg/L (Smith et al., 2018). In parallel, changes in hydrophobicity were measured using the water drop penetration time test on dried, homogenized samples of each treatment.

Physico-chemical Analysis:
To comprehensively analyze BC effects, the physico-chemical properties of each BC type were characterized before and after soil amendment. Analytical techniques included Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) for functional group identification, Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) analysis for surface area measurement, and scanning electron microscopy (SEM) for morphological examination. Pyrolysis impact over BC structural characteristics was quantified based on functional groups and pore architecture modifications.

Statistical Analysis:
Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.0.5). Sorption data underwent analysis of variance (ANOVA) to identify significant differences across treatments, with BC feedstock type and pyrolysis temperature as fixed factors. Tukey's Honestly Significant Difference (HSD) test provided post-hoc comparisons to elucidate pairwise differences between treatments (P < 0.05). Correlation analysis further explored relationships between BC properties (e.g., surface area, hydrophobicity level) and DMPP sorption.

Control treatments involving non-amended soils were incorporated to establish baseline sorption behavior, aiding the discernment of BC-specific effects. Deductions from the statistical outputs were corroborated through linear regression models built to predict DMPP sorption based on BC attributes.

Validation and Quality Control:
Quality control was pursued through repeated trials under identical conditions to ensure the reliability of experimental outcomes. Also, pre-experiment equipment calibration and periodic checks guaranteed precision and accuracy in chemical analyses. Detailed inspection of sorption data, including outlier assessments and normality tests, verified data integrity and adherence to assumptions required for ANOVA tests.

This methodology, encompassing soil type, BC characterization, sorption studies, and comprehensive statistical analyses, was integral for achieving a thorough understanding of DMPP dynamics within BC-amended soil environments. The study's robust design facilitated the generation of conclusive evidence concerning the role of BC properties in nitrogen inhibitor sorption, contributing to the broader discourse on BC's role in sustainable soil management.

Results

The experiment conducted was designed to examine the sorption behavior of the nitrification inhibitor 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate (DMPP) in soils amended with biochar (BC), and the effects of various biochar properties on DMPP sorption. Our analysis focused on the quantitative changes in DMPP sorption when biochar was added to the soil, considering different pyrolysis temperatures and feedstock types used to produce biochar. The findings of this study offer insights into biochar’s role in improving the effectiveness of DMPP as a nitrification inhibitor in agricultural settings.

The soils used in this study were amended with biochar produced from three different feedstocks: miscanthus, rice husk, and wood chips, each subjected to different pyrolysis temperatures (300°C, 500°C, and 700°C). After 15 months of aging, the mixtures underwent sorption tests to determine the impact of the biochar on DMPP interception.

Results showed that biochar application generally enhanced DMPP sorption in soil, with variable results depending significantly on the type of feedstock and the pyrolysis temperature applied. Biochar derived from miscanthus showed the highest increase in DMPP sorption compared to the control soil with no biochar, reflecting an average increment of 35% at a pyrolysis temperature of 300°C, 28% at 500°C, and 25% at 700°C. This suggests that miscanthus-based biochar, particularly when pyrolyzed at lower temperatures, may be most effective in enhancing DMPP retention in soil. The enhanced sorption at lower pyrolysis temperatures was statistically significant (p < 0.05) when compared to higher pyrolysis temperatures.

Rice husk biochar increased DMPP sorption by an average of 22% at 300°C, 18% at 500°C, and 15% at 700°C. The reduction in efficacy with increased pyrolysis temperature suggests that lower temperature pyrolysis preserves more of the organic functional groups conducive to sorption processes. This was evident from Fourier Transform Infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy, which indicated a higher presence of aromatic and phenolic compounds at lower pyrolysis temperatures, potentially contributing to increased interaction sites for DMPP.

Wood chip biochar showed more modest results, enhancing DMPP sorption by 18% at 300°C, 12% at 500°C, and a negligible 5% at 700°C. The lowest sorption increase at the highest temperature underscore the conclusion that pyrolysis conditions can significantly affect biochar's structural properties, such as surface area and porosity, which influence its sorption capabilities. Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) analysis revealed a 40% decrease in surface area for wood chip biochar as pyrolysis temperature increased from 300°C to 700°C, which correlates with reduced sorption effectiveness.

Furthermore, the aged biochar-soil mixtures displayed altered hydrophobic properties. Contact angle measurement suggested increased hydrophilicity in soil amended with biochar. Soils with miscanthus biochar at 300°C exhibited a contact angle reduction from 58° (control) to 42°, correlating with enhanced DMPP sorption. Similar patterns were observed for rice husk and wood chip biochars, indicating the role of biochar-induced changes in soil hydrophobicity in facilitating DMPP sorption.

The influence of biochar feedstock and pyrolysis temperature also extended to the cation exchange capacity (CEC) of the soil-biochar mixtures. CEC was found to be increased by 20% in miscanthus biochar at 300°C compared to control soils, potentially improving the soil’s ability to retain nutrient ions, including DMPP. In contrast, wood chip biochar at 700°C showed only a marginal increase (5%) in CEC, reflecting the diminished sorption capacity seen in prior analyses.

These findings underscore the capacity of biochar to alter soil physico-chemical properties which are instrumental to the sorption behavior of DMPP. The enhanced sorption of DMPP, particularly with miscanthus biochar pyrolyzed at lower temperatures, indicates a promising avenue for optimizing nitrification inhibitor efficacy in biochar-amended soils. Future studies may focus on exploring other feedstock types and further elucidating the interaction mechanisms between biochar components and DMPP to fine-tune biochar application for improved soil management and environmental sustainability in agriculture.

## Discussion and Conclusion

The findings of this study provide insightful revelations on the interplay between biochar (BC) application and the sorption dynamics of the nitrification inhibitor 3,4-dimethylpyrazole phosphate (DMPP) in soil systems. The enhanced sorption of DMPP in the presence of BC offers a promising method to moderate nitrogen cycling in agricultural soils, particularly as BC amendments continue to gain traction for improving soil health and mitigating climate change (Lehmann and Joseph, 2015). However, our results also underscore the complexity of soil-BC interactions and the necessity for a nuanced understanding of how BC characteristics influence its efficacy as a sorption medium.

The observed variation in DMPP sorption as influenced by BC feedstock type and pyrolysis temperature highlights the critical role of BC's physicochemical properties. Our study confirms that BC pyrolyzed at lower temperatures tends to increase DMPP sorption. This could be attributed to higher levels of surface area and porosity typically associated with low-temperature BC (Singh et al., 2010), which potentially enhance the adsorption sites available for DMPP. Furthermore, the surface functional groups prevalent in these BCs might facilitate stronger interactions with DMPP molecules, as compared to those produced at higher temperatures, which often have reduced functional group densities due to more complete carbonization.

The influence of BC on soil hydrophobicity emerged as a significant factor in DMPP sorption. Increased hydrophobic domains in soil-BC mixtures can lead to preferential partitioning of hydrophobic compounds like DMPP, enhancing its retention in soil (Buss et al., 2012). Nonetheless, the degree of hydrophobicity is contingent upon BC's inherent properties, accentuating the need for selecting appropriate BC types based on their intended agricultural application and the specific environmental context.

Despite these promising outcomes, the study faces certain limitations. Firstly, the inherent variability of soil types and properties across different regions may limit the generalizability of our findings. Soils with distinct mineral compositions, organic matter content, and pH could exhibit different interactions with BC and DMPP, thus necessitating field-specific empirical studies to supplement our current laboratory-based approach. Additionally, the aging of BC in soil was standardized to 15 months in our experiments; however, the sorption dynamics of DMPP and the stability of BC properties over longer periods remain unexplored. Long-term field studies are required to investigate the persistence and effectiveness of DMPP sorption in real-world conditions.

The implications of enhanced DMPP sorption in BC-amended soils are multifaceted. Primarily, it presents a viable strategy to curb the accelerated emission of nitrous oxide (N2O) associated with BC applications. By effectively delaying the nitrification process, DMPP can reduce nitrogen losses, improving nitrogen use efficiency and ultimately contributing to more sustainable agricultural practices (Zaman et al., 2013). This is particularly pertinent in light of global efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and address climate change, as curbing N2O emissions can have a substantial impact given its potent greenhouse effect (Ravishankara et al., 2009).

Furthermore, our findings have implications for the management of fertilizer inputs in BC-amended soils. With improved retention of nitrification inhibitors like DMPP, farmers may be able to optimize the timing and quantity of fertilizer applications, thus reducing costs and minimizing the potential for environmental contamination. However, it is essential to balance the increased availability of ammonium with the potential for enhanced ammonia volatilization, a factor that was not directly addressed in our study but warrants further investigation.

In conclusion, the strategic application of BC to enhance DMPP sorption presents a promising avenue for increasing nitrogen use efficiency in agricultural soils. Our study elucidates the critical influence of BC properties—particularly those influenced by pyrolysis temperature—on its functionality as a sorption medium. While the results are promising, they underscore the importance of understanding the nuanced interactions within soil-BC systems to optimize agricultural outcomes. Future research should focus on field-scale verification of these interactions, considering long-term effects and a broader range of soil types, to fully harness the potential of BC as a tool for sustainable agriculture.

### Introduction

The modern lifestyle has increasingly shifted towards prolonged sedentary behaviors due to technological advancements and changes in occupational demands. This shift is exemplified by the significant amount of time adults spend sitting throughout the day, whether at work, during transportation, or at home engaging in passive leisure activities such as watching television or using digital devices (Dunstan et al., 2012). Empirical studies have demonstrated that adults spend over half of their waking hours in sedentary activities, specifically sitting (Matthews et al., 2008). Consequentially, this raises public health concerns due to emerging evidence linking excessive sedentary behavior to various adverse health outcomes, notably cardiometabolic risk factors such as obesity, dyslipidemia, hypertension, and insulin resistance (Hamilton et al., 2007).

Cardiometabolic diseases, including cardiovascular maladies and Type 2 diabetes, have substantial implications for global morbidity and mortality rates. Indeed, these conditions have been implicated in the majority of non-communicable disease burdens worldwide (World Health Organization, 2014). Understanding modifiable lifestyle factors that contribute to these diseases is essential for developing effective prevention and intervention strategies. While sedentary behavior has been extensively studied as an independent risk factor for cardiometabolic health (Tremblay et al., 2010), the nuanced relationship between sitting time and these risk factors requires further investigation, particularly when considering other influential variables such as physical fitness.

Cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) represents a vital determinant of overall health, reflecting the efficiency of the cardiovascular and respiratory systems in supplying oxygen during sustained physical activity. High levels of CRF are associated with decreased all-cause mortality and reduced risk of cardiovascular diseases (Kodama et al., 2009). However, the question of whether CRF can mitigate the risks associated with prolonged sedentary behavior remains an area of active research. Some evidence suggests that high CRF may counteract some of the negative effects of sedentary behavior on metabolic health, whereas others contend that excessive sitting time poses a risk independently of physical fitness levels (Ekelund et al., 2016).

Despite considerable research into sedentary behavior and its effects on cardiometabolic health, there remain gaps in our understanding. Past investigations have frequently failed to account for CRF when examining the relationship between sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors. This omission poses a significant limitation, as CRF may modify the effect of sedentary behavior on health outcomes or confound observed associations. Furthermore, gender-based differences in these relationships have not been extensively explored, leaving a critical gap in our understanding (Healy et al., 2008).

Our study aims to address these gaps by examining the association between sitting time and various cardiometabolic risk factors with CRF taken into account. Specifically, we aim to understand whether adjusting for CRF alters the association between sitting time and indicators of obesity, blood lipids, glucose metabolism, and blood pressure. Additionally, we explore potential gender-based differences in these associations, recognizing that behavioral and physiological responses to sedentary behavior and physical activity may differ between men and women.

By utilizing data from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study, an extensive dataset that includes comprehensive health and fitness assessments, we leverage robust, objective measures to assess the interactions between sitting time, CRF, and cardiometabolic risk factors. This study employs a cross-sectional design spanning from 2010 to 2013, incorporating data from over 6,000 participants, and constituting one of the largest efforts to delineate these relationships comprehensively. Our findings are expected to contribute to the existing literature by clarifying the interplay between sedentary lifestyle and physical fitness and their combined impact on cardiometabolic health.

In conclusion, the primary objectives of this investigation are: (1) to assess the independent association between sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors after adjusting for CRF, and (2) to explore gender-based differences in these associations. Our study promises to advance current understanding by tackling the confounding and modifying roles of CRF, thereby offering insights into potential strategies for managing cardiometabolic risk through lifestyle modifications. Health professionals and policymakers can utilize these findings to devise comprehensive physical activity guidelines that encompass both reductions in sedentary time and enhancements in physical fitness, aimed at improving cardiometabolic health on a population scale.

## Methods

In the present study, we performed a cross-sectional analysis to investigate the association between sitting time and various cardiometabolic risk factors while adjusting for cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). The study population was sourced from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study (CCLS), which is known for its extensive data on cardiovascular and metabolic health parameters collected in a consistent and standardized manner.

**Data and Study Design**

Our analysis included data collected between 2010 and 2013 from participants who underwent comprehensive medical examinations at the Cooper Clinic in Dallas, Texas. We initially considered a sample size consisting of 4,486 men and 1,845 women, aged 20 to 79 years, who reported their daily estimated sitting time. To ensure high-quality data regarding physical fitness and health metrics, participants in this study had to meet several inclusion criteria: they had undergone measures of adiposity (including waist girth and body fat percentage), blood lipid profiles (including total cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein [HDL], and low-density lipoprotein [LDL] cholesterol), fasting glucose levels, and blood pressure, and had completed a maximal exercise treadmill test to evaluate CRF.

Exclusion criteria for this study included a history of cardiovascular disease, type 2 diabetes, or any major health issues that could significantly alter CRF or influence sitting time (such as severe orthopedic limitations). Individuals with incomplete data or who failed to complete the maximal treadmill test were also excluded.

**Procedures**

Sitting time was self-reported by participants as part of a larger health questionnaire which queried average daily time spent sitting on weekdays and weekends in hours or as a percentage of the day. CRF was estimated based on VO2 max, which was derived from the duration of a maximal graded exercise stress test conducted on a treadmill. This testing protocol has been previously validated and correlates strongly with direct measures of VO2 max (Maciejczyk et al., 2018).

Adiposity measures were obtained during the clinic visit using standardized measurement techniques. Waist circumference was measured at the level of the iliac crest with participants standing, and body fat percentage was assessed via air displacement plethysmography (Wang et al., 2000). Blood samples were drawn following a minimum 12-hour overnight fast. Lipid profiles, including total cholesterol, HDL, and LDL, were analyzed using enzymatic methods standardized in the Cooper Clinic laboratories. Blood glucose was determined through the glucose oxidase method.

**Statistical Analysis**

The primary analytical approach involved logistic regression modeling to estimate the odds ratios (ORs) for associations between sitting time and dichotomous cardiometabolic outcomes: obesity, dyslipidemia, hyperglycemia, and hypertension. For each outcome, logistic regression models were adjusted for confounders including age, sex, race/ethnicity, smoking status, alcohol intake, dietary patterns, and CRF levels, which were categorized into tertiles based on age- and sex-specific norms (“high,” “moderate,” and “low” CRF).

Effect modification by CRF was investigated by including interaction terms between CRF (tertile) and sitting time (categorized as “almost none of the time,” “some of the time,” and “almost all of the time”). CRF was modeled as a potential confounder a priori, given its significant correlation with both sedentary behavior and cardiometabolic health outcomes (Ross et al., 2016). We further explored potential nonlinear relationships and thresholds effects between predicted cardiometabolic risk and sitting time through fitting regression splines.

Each of the cardiometabolic risk factors was analyzed separately for men and women due to prior evidence suggesting sex-specific differences in sedentary behavior and metabolic responses (Ding et al., 2017). Adequacy of model fit was assessed using the Hosmer-Lemeshow goodness-of-fit test, and multicollinearity was checked via variance inflation factors (VIFs), with all VIFs maintained below 2.0.

Sensitivity analyses were performed by running logistic regressions with alternative definitions of sitting, such as quartiles of sitting duration, and by excluding participants with chronic conditions that might influence sitting time other than those explicitly accounted for in the models. All analyses were conducted using SAS software (version 9.4; SAS Institute Inc., Cary, NC), and statistical significance was considered at a p-value less than 0.05.

Given the cross-sectional design, limitations inherent in this study should be acknowledged, such as the dependence on self-reported data for sitting time which could introduce recall bias, and the inability to infer causality between sedentary time and cardiometabolic outcomes. Nonetheless, this analysis serves to extend literature on the interplay between sedentary behavior and metabolic health, particularly accounting for the robust measure of objective CRF.

These methodological steps provide a clear roadmap for our analysis, aiming to distinguish the independent contributions of sitting time to cardiometabolic risk beyond that explained by CRF. While our focus was primarily on these associations, considerations of broader lifestyle interventions remain imperative for comprehensive health promotion strategies.

Results

The results of our study provide an in-depth examination of the associations between sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors, after adjusting for cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF). Our dataset included a total of 6,331 participants, with 4,486 men and 1,845 women, who provided complete data on daily sitting time and underwent maximal stress testing to assess CRF, along with measurements for adiposity, blood lipids, glucose, and blood pressure.

The first analyses focused on men, who were stratified into categories of sitting time based on their self-reports ranging from minimal sitting (almost none of the time) to maximal sitting (almost all of the time). Our logistic regression models controlled for age, smoking status, alcohol consumption, and CRF. The results indicated a significant association between sitting time and obesity in men. Specifically, men who reported sitting almost all of the time exhibited an increased likelihood of being classified as obese by waist girth, with an odds ratio (OR) of 2.61 (95% confidence interval [CI], 1.25–5.47) compared to men who sat almost none of the time. Similarly, when obesity was defined by percentage of body fat, men who reported sitting almost all of the time had an OR of 3.33 (95% CI, 1.35–8.20), suggesting more than a threefold increase in the likelihood of obesity compared to their least sedentary counterparts.

Further stratification of the male cohort by CRF levels revealed that the relationship between sitting time and obesity persisted even among men with moderate-to-high CRF, underscoring the independent effect of sitting time on adiposity. However, no significant associations were observed between sitting time and other cardiometabolic risk factors, such as dyslipidemia (e.g., elevated low-density lipoprotein cholesterol or triglycerides), impaired fasting glucose, or hypertension, after adjusting for CRF levels. This suggests that CRF may moderate the effects of prolonged sedentary behavior on these specific risk factors in men, as indicated by the non-significant interaction terms between sitting time and CRF level (p > 0.05).

In contrast, the analysis for women did not reveal significant associations between sitting time and any of the cardiometabolic risk factors studied, including measures of adiposity, when adjusted for CRF and other covariates. The absence of significant findings in women may be indicative of sex-specific differences in the physiological impact of sitting behavior, or differences in the nature of sedentary activities typically undertaken by women versus men. The logistic regression model yielded ORs close to null for obesity, blood lipid irregularities, impaired glucose, and blood pressure irregularities (all p-values > 0.05), suggesting a negligible impact of sitting time when CRF is accounted for.

To further analyze the relationship between sitting time and CRF, additional subgroup analyses were performed examining men and women separately across tertiles of CRF. In lower CRF tertiles, the detrimental effects of increased sitting time on obesity measures were more pronounced among male participants, whereas such trends were not evident in the higher CRF tertiles, supporting the concept that maintaining a higher level of CRF may mitigate some of the adverse effects associated with prolonged sitting. For women, however, sitting time did not exhibit any significant interaction with CRF tertiles, reinforcing previous observations of the study's main findings.

This study's strength lies in its robust dataset and the comprehensive adjustment for CRF—a known confounder in physical activity research. Despite the lack of significant findings for women, our results have highlighted the potential for reducing sitting time as a feasible intervention strategy to combat obesity in men. Continuous monitoring of sitting patterns using objective measures such as accelerometers could provide more detailed insights into the specific contexts in which sedentary behaviors exacerbate health risks, particularly for certain demographic groups.

In summary, our findings suggest a sex-specific interaction between prolonged sitting time and cardiometabolic risk factors, predominantly affecting adiposity among men. This emphasizes the critical role of integrating both physical activity and reduced sitting time into public health guidelines aimed at reducing obesity and enhancing cardio-metabolic health, with targeted interventions potentially more beneficial for males as per the data available from the Cooper Center Longitudinal Study.

Discussion and Conclusion

The present study expands on the evolving area of research exploring the relationship between sedentary behavior, specifically sitting time, and cardiometabolic risk factors, emphasizing the role of cardiorespiratory fitness (CRF) as a potential confounding or modifying factor. Our findings suggest that for men, extended sitting time is significantly associated with increased adiposity, as evidenced by waist girth and percentage body fat, even after adjusting for CRF. However, the anticipated associations between sitting time and other cardiometabolic risk factors such as blood lipids, glucose levels, and blood pressure largely dissipated post adjustment for CRF. Interestingly, for women, sitting time did not exhibit significant associations with any of the cardiometabolic risk factors after controlling for CRF and additional covariates.

These results underscore the complexity of interactions between sitting time, CRF, and cardiometabolic health outcomes. It is evident from our study that CRF plays a critical role in mediating the relationship between sedentary behavior and health risks, aligning with previous research which posits CRF as a protective factor against cardiometabolic dysfunction (Lee et al., 2012; Swift et al., 2013). Among men, even when CRF was accounted for, prolonged sitting was independently associated with obesity, suggesting that reducing sitting time might be a viable strategy to mitigate obesity risk. However, this relationship was not observed for other risk factors, indicating that CRF might overshadow the impact of sitting time in these domains.

In contrast, the absence of significant associations among women highlights potential sex-specific differences in how sedentary behaviors influence cardiometabolic health. This discrepancy may be attributed to variances in fat distribution patterns, hormonal influences, and social factors affecting physical activity engagement between genders (Tremblay et al., 2010). Moreover, the modulation by CRF suggests that interventions aiming to improve physical fitness should be pivotal, especially for women, when designing strategies to curtail sedentary lifestyles and their potential health repercussions.

Several limitations should be acknowledged in interpreting our findings. Firstly, the cross-sectional nature of the study inhibits the establishment of causal relationships. Longitudinal studies are necessary to delineate the temporal sequence and causality between sitting time, CRF, and cardiometabolic risk factors. Secondly, self-reported sitting time introduces potential biases related to recall inaccuracies and subjective interpretation of sedentary behaviors. Objective measures, such as accelerometry, could enhance precision and reliability in capturing true sedentary time. Thirdly, our study cohort primarily comprised healthy, middle-aged adults, possibly limiting generalizability to younger or older populations and those with existing health conditions.

The implications of these findings are multifaceted. As sedentary behavior becomes increasingly prevalent in modern society, accentuated by technological advancements and occupational demands, public health initiatives should prioritize strategies to reduce sedentary time, particularly among men as indicated by our results. Interventions could incorporate environmental modifications (e.g., sit-stand desks), educational programs emphasizing the risks associated with prolonged sitting, and community-based physical activity campaigns that foster active lifestyles. Additionally, enhancing CRF through regular physical activity remains an indispensable component of these interventions, given its overarching protective role against cardiometabolic risks.

For women, more nuanced approaches may be necessary. Given the lack of association between sitting time and cardiometabolic outcomes post CRF adjustment in our findings, strategies should potentially allocate more emphasis on improving overall physical fitness rather than solely focusing on reducing sedentary periods. Nevertheless, gender-specific research should be pursued to better understand these differences and refine intervention frameworks accordingly.

In conclusion, our study contributes valuable insights into the differential impact of sitting time on cardiometabolic health contingent on CRF levels and highlights the essential integration of fitness enhancement in mitigating sedentary behavior risks. Though reductions in sitting time appear beneficial for lowering obesity risk, the broader cardiometabolic benefits may heavily rely on the interplay with CRF. Further longitudinal studies and gender-specific investigations are critical to advancing our understanding and fostering effective public health strategies.

## Introduction

In recent decades, the issue of school exclusion, also commonly referred to as suspension, has garnered considerable attention from educational researchers, policy makers, and practitioners alike. School exclusion is a disciplinary measure imposed on students for breaches of conduct, resulting in their temporary removal from classroom instruction and, in some cases, from school premises altogether (Whitford & Levine‐Donnerstein, 2014). As schools are critical socialization agents—second only to families in their influence—they bear the dual responsibility of fostering academic achievement and upholding social discipline. Hence, the effects of exclusionary policies not only impact immediate educational outcomes but also have long-term implications for students' social and economic trajectories (Maimon, Antonaccio, & French, 2012).

The prevailing corpus of research unequivocally indicates the adverse fallout of school exclusions. Students who experience suspensions are more susceptible to academic failure, diminished graduation rates, and subsequent involvement in antisocial or criminal activities (Arcia, 2006). Moreover, the suspension is often a precursor to entanglement with the juvenile justice system, thereby enmeshing young individuals in cycles of punitive control that restrict future opportunities for gaining skills and employment (Townsend, 2000). Economically, the repercussions extend beyond the individual, imposing substantial costs on taxpayers and society at large due to the increased likelihood of future social service needs and lower lifetime earnings potential among excluded students (Hemphill et al., 2006).

Concurrently, school exclusions reveal profound inequities entrenched within educational systems. Empirical evidence underscores that such disciplinary actions disproportionately affect males, ethnic minorities, and students from economically disadvantaged or special educational needs backgrounds (Skiba et al., 2002). These disparities not only violate principles of educational equity but potentially exacerbate existing social inequalities, further marginalising already vulnerable groups. Despite these insights, school exclusion persists as a disciplinary measure, highlighting a pressing need for effective interventions.

Several programs have been implemented over the years with the aim of mitigating school exclusion rates. These initiatives, which range from enhancing academic skills to providing counseling and mentoring, and skills training for teachers, have demonstrated varying degrees of success. However, to date, there has been a lack of comprehensive syntheses regarding their overall efficacy. Previous reviews have often been fragmented, focusing on localized interventions without appraising the broader landscape of preventative measures across different educational contexts (Wilson, Lipsey, & Derzon, 2003).

Against this backdrop, the present systematic review seeks to bridge this knowledge gap by assembling evidence from randomised controlled trials (RCTs) evaluating school-based interventions aimed at reducing exclusion rates. Our approach prioritizes a methodologically rigorous design to ensure reliable estimation of intervention impacts. As the first systematic review of its kind, this study will not only quantify the efficacy of various intervention types but will also explore moderating factors that potentially influence intervention outcomes, such as participant demographics, the theoretical underpinnings of interventions, and implementation quality.

The central research question driving this review is: “Do school-based interventions reduce the use of exclusionary sanctions in schools?” In examining this, the study also seeks to discern the relative effectiveness of different intervention approaches. To this end, we will compare the impacts of interventions such as the enhancement of academic skills, counselling, and mentoring/monitoring, as well as skills training for teachers. Additionally, we aim to delineate the role of contextual factors such as age, gender, and ethnicity of participants in shaping intervention efficacy.

Furthermore, this review aspires to address the methodological heterogeneity observed across studies by evaluating whether characteristics specific to intervention design, implementation fidelity, and evaluator involvement consistently affect outcomes. For example, concerns have been raised that independent evaluators may report lower effect sizes compared to those involved in intervention design, highlighting potential biases needing empirical clarification (Lipsey, 1990).

In terms of contributions, this review holds significant promise for both theoretical development and practical application in educational settings. Theoretically, it seeks to challenge and refine prevailing assumptions regarding the universality and translatability of intervention efficacy by situating its findings within a broader sociocultural context. Practically, the study provides policymakers and educators with evidence-based recommendations that can inform the design and implementation of future disciplinary practices, steering them toward interventions proven to be effective at reducing school exclusion.

Ultimately, the findings aim to aid the development of more equitable and effective educational policies and practices, contributing to a reduction in exclusion-related disparities and ameliorating long-term adverse outcomes for at-risk student populations. This endeavor not only advances the scholarly discourse on school discipline but also holds implications for broader social justice endeavors within the educational system.

## Methods

The methodological framework for this systematic review was designed to rigorously evaluate the efficacy of school-based interventions in reducing disciplinary school exclusions. This process consisted of several key components, including data sources and inclusion criteria, study design and procedures, and statistical analysis methods.

### Data Sources and Inclusion Criteria

The initial phase of this research involved a comprehensive search for relevant studies that were published from 1980 onwards. Twenty-seven databases, including both published and unpublished literature repositories such as ERIC, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane Library, were systematically explored. Searches were conducted from September 1 to December 1, 2015. In addition to database searches, targeted efforts were made to identify further studies through expert consultations, assessments of citation lists from previous reviews, and searching conference proceedings (Higgins & Green, 2011). This extensive search strategy yielded a total of 42,749 references.

Studies were deemed eligible for inclusion if they met specific pre-established criteria. They needed to evaluate school-based or school-supported interventions aimed at reducing suspension rates and should target school-aged children between four and 18 years of age, regardless of nationality or social background. Moreover, only randomized controlled trials (RCTs) with at least one experimental group and one control or placebo group were considered for inclusion, as these provide the highest quality evidence for intervention efficacy (Borenstein et al., 2009).

### Study Design and Procedures

The identification and selection of studies followed a rigorous two-stage screening process. Initially, references were screened based on titles, abstracts, and key terms, which narrowed the pool to 1,474 potential studies. An additional 22 references were obtained through other sources, bringing the total to 1,496 references after removing duplicates. Two independent researchers then reviewed the full texts of these articles to determine final eligibility, resulting in the exclusion of 1,459 papers and the inclusion of 37 studies deemed suitable for meta-analysis.

Each study's methodological quality was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) tool, a validated instrument for evaluating risk of bias in RCTs (Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care, 2015). Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved through discussion, ensuring a rigorous evaluation of study quality.

### Statistical Analysis

The statistical analysis involved meta-analysis conducted under a random-effects model, which accounts for variability both within and between studies, offering a more conservative estimate of effect sizes (DerSimonian & Laird, 1986). The main outcome metric was the standardized mean difference (SMD) with accompanying 95% confidence intervals (CIs), derived from reported effect sizes of the intervention on exclusion rates. Results were visually represented through forest plots.

Subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the differential effects of the interventions on various types of exclusions, such as in-school versus out-of-school exclusions. Additionally, four intervention categories—enhancement of academic skills, counselling, mentoring/monitoring, and teachers’ skills training—were specifically analyzed due to their prominence in the literature.

To assess the impact of potential moderators—such as participants’ characteristics, theoretical bases, and quality of interventions—meta-regression analyses were conducted. These analyses aimed to explain the observed heterogeneity in intervention effects across studies. Variables were entered into the models as exploratory moderators to assess whether they significantly influenced outcomes.

Publication bias was a concern, given the reliance on published studies. Funnel plots were used to visually inspect the presence of asymmetries in study distribution, and Duval and Tweedie’s trim-and-fill procedure was adopted to adjust for potential publication bias and assess its impact on the pooled estimates (Duval & Tweedie, 2000).

### Conclusion

This comprehensive methodological approach ensured that the systematic review and meta-analysis were conducted with a high level of rigor and transparency. The synthesis of evidence was aimed at providing policymakers and educational practitioners with robust conclusions on the effectiveness of different school-based interventions for reducing disciplinary exclusions. Through careful selection and analysis processes, our study contributes meaningful insights toward understanding and addressing this critical issue in education.

Results

The systematic review and meta-analysis incorporated findings from 37 studies, with the overwhelming majority emanating from the United States (n=33), a smaller subset from the United Kingdom (n=3), and one study with an unspecified origin. Analysis of the interventions demonstrated a small but statistically significant reduction in school exclusion rates, with a standardized mean difference (SMD) of 0.30 and a 95% confidence interval (CI) ranging from 0.20 to 0.41 (p<0.001). These results imply that students participating in these interventions experienced a reduced likelihood of being subject to suspension compared to those in control or placebo groups. It is noteworthy that this outcome was most profound during the immediate period extending up to six months following the intervention.

In contrast, when assessing the longevity of the interventions' effects, defined as twelve months or more post-intervention, the outcomes were less encouraging. The effectiveness markedly diminished, with an SMD of 0.15 and a 95% CI from -0.06 to 0.35, ultimately lacking statistical significance. This decline suggests that while the interventions offer a temporary reprieve from exclusionaries, the long-term benefits are minimal and statistically indistinguishable from zero.

The review also evaluated the efficacy of interventions across different exclusion typologies—expulsion, in-school exclusion, and out-of-school exclusion. Interventions showed marked success in reducing expulsion and in-school exclusion (SMDs not specified due to the broad nature of reported results), indicating a potential focus area for future programmatic efforts. Conversely, the effect on out-of-school exclusion was negligible and failed to achieve statistical significance, reflecting an apparent challenge in modifying behaviors contributing to this exclusion form.

Among the interventions, nine distinct types were cataloged, with four presenting statistically significant positive results. These are enhancement of academic skills (study numbers allocated unspecified), counseling, mentoring/monitoring, and teacher skills training. However, each subtype had a limited representation in the dataset, cautioning against broad generalization of these promising outcomes. For example, skills training for teachers demonstrated effectiveness in fostering an environment less conducive to exclusionary practices, yet its SMDs were susceptible to variance based on limited sample sizes.

In exploring heterogeneity sources, predefined moderators encompassing participants’ demographic and psychological characteristics failed to elucidate differences across study results. Likewise, interventions’ theoretical underpinnings and implementation quality did not emerge as effective explanatory factors. Post-hoc analysis, however, identified the evaluator's role as a significant moderator: interventions assessed by independent evaluators showed reduced effect sizes compared to those where evaluators were involved in the intervention design and implementation (SMDs and CIs unspecified). This potentially indicates an experimental bias warranting consideration in future evaluations.

The analyses also confronted publication bias implications. Funnel plot visual assessment, alongside Duval and Tweedie's trim-and-fill procedure, suggested that the reported effect sizes might be slightly inflated. Thus, while the overall positive assessment remains, it should be interpreted within the confines of potential bias influences.

In summation, this investigation underscores a pressing need for more comprehensive and varied geographical studies to verify these conclusions within different educative frameworks and cultural contexts. Despite early positive indications, the outcomes call for cautious optimism, demanding rigorous, long-term follow-ups to substantiate the interventions' sustained impact. Moreover, nuanced exploration of intervention-specific factors and a critical appraisal of evaluator neutrality is recommended to refine program efficacy assessments in future research trajectories.

**Discussion and Conclusion**

The present systematic review provides a critical evaluation of school-based interventions aimed at reducing disciplinary school exclusions, drawing from an evidence base of 37 randomized controlled trials primarily conducted in the USA, with a few in the UK. Our findings offer pivotal insights into the efficacy of various intervention strategies over short and medium-term periods. While the overall impact of these interventions is modest, there are discernible differences in effectiveness linked to the type of intervention employed.

Primarily, the results indicate that interventions such as enhancement of academic skills, counselling, mentoring/monitoring, and skills training for teachers have a significant and desirable impact on reducing exclusion rates, particularly when assessed shortly after implementation. These strategies appear to address core issues related to students' behavior and engagement while providing teachers with the skills necessary to manage and mitigate disruptive behavior in constructive ways. Notably, the effectiveness of these interventions was more pronounced for more severe forms of exclusion, such as expulsion and in-school exclusion, compared to out-of-school exclusion.

However, the sustainability of these effects raises concerns. Our analysis reveals a diminution in the impact of interventions over the long term, with effects failing to sustain significance beyond six months post-intervention. This attenuation suggests a pressing need for continuous support and possibly booster sessions to maintain positive outcomes. Further, the negligible impact of these programs on reducing antisocial behavior underscores a potential area where school-based interventions might be supplemented with broader community or home-based programs that address the wider social influences on behavior (Wasserman et al., 2015).

The evaluation of moderator variables yielded limited insights, revealing no substantial evidence that participants' characteristics or the theoretical underpinnings of interventions explain variations in effect sizes. This suggests the need for a more nuanced understanding of the complex and multifaceted nature of school exclusions, possibly requiring a closer examination of contextual factors such as school culture, socio-economic status, and community resources (Mallett, 2016).

One notable finding pertains to the influence of evaluator involvement. Interventions assessed by independent teams reported lower effect sizes compared to those evaluated by teams involved in the intervention's design and delivery, suggesting a potential bias that could inflate the perceived effectiveness of interventions (Cheung & Slavin, 2016). This calls for more rigorous methodological designs and independent evaluations in future research to mitigate bias and provide more reliable estimates of intervention impacts.

Despite the review's strengths in consolidating evidence across multiple studies, several limitations must be acknowledged. The primary limitation is the overrepresentation of studies conducted in the USA, limiting the generalizability of the findings to other educational contexts with potentially different disciplinary frameworks and cultures. Moreover, the limited number of studies for each sub-type of intervention necessitates cautious interpretation of results, stressing the need for further research to validate these findings across diverse settings and populations.

The implications for policy and practice from this review are manifold. Policymakers should consider investing in school-based programs that integrate academic support, counselling, and skills training for both students and teachers. Importantly, these interventions need to be part of a sustained, multi-tiered approach that includes regular follow-ups and adaptations to maintain improvements over time. Interventions must also be culturally sensitive and adaptable to the specific needs of varying student populations to maximize their effectiveness and equitability (Gregory et al., 2010).

Furthermore, the lack of impact on antisocial behavior highlights an opportunity for integrating complementary strategies that extend beyond the school environment. Engaging families and communities in cultivating supportive environments might compound the benefits realized from school-based interventions, fostering holistic development and long-term behavioral improvements (Bryan et al., 2012).

In conclusion, while the reviewed interventions appear to wield modest immediate effects in reducing school exclusions, there remains significant scope for enhancing the sustainability and impact of these measures. The integration of robust, bias-mitigating research methodologies and consideration of contextual and demographic variability is paramount for realizing more effective and inclusive solutions. Future research should prioritize diversifying the geographic representation of studies and exploring innovative intervention designs that incorporate multi-faceted approaches for comprehensive behavior management.

Introduction

Planetary exploration has undergone significant transformations over the past decades, transitioning from telescopic observations to complex robotic missions that provide unprecedented insights into the celestial bodies within our solar system. Among these endeavors, the exploration of Mars holds particular scientific importance due to its proximity and similarities to Earth, potential for past habitability, and the quest for extant or extinct life (McEwen et al., 2011). The Mars rover missions, spearheaded by agencies such as NASA and ESA, have been pivotal in our understanding of the Martian landscape, climate, and geology. These missions have returned vast troves of data, including over 22 million images that serve as primary sources for scientific analyses (Grotzinger et al., 2005).

However, the acquisition of such a massive volume of data from Mars presents challenges. Despite advancements in rover technology, the process of capturing and transmitting images relies heavily on human-led operations, which encompass task planning and anomaly detection. Human experts, based on their domain expertise and scientific interest, generally predetermine the path the rovers take and the phenomena to capture. While this method has substantially contributed to mission successes, it limits the potential for real-time decision-making due to inherent time delays in communication between Earth and Mars (Arvidson et al., 2014). In addition, only a fraction of captured data can be transmitted to Earth because of bandwidth constraints and the need to prioritize relevant scientific information (Squyres et al., 2003).

Given these constraints, there is a critical gap in the current planetary exploration methodologies that inhibit timely and autonomous responsiveness to unexpected or rare scientific phenomena. Autonomous systems in planetary exploration have shown promise, particularly in navigation and hazard avoidance (Bajracharya et al., 2008), yet the proactive identification of scientifically valuable content within acquired images remains a challenge. This deficiency underscores the necessity for solutions that integrate intelligent systems capable of autonomously identifying and prioritizing scientific features of interest.

In recent years, the advent of artificial intelligence (AI) and deep learning methodologies has presented new opportunities for enhancing the autonomy of robotic systems. Particularly, deep image captioning networks have demonstrated the ability to generate descriptive captions of visual content with substantial accuracy (Vinyals et al., 2015). These networks enable machines to interpret and describe complex scenes, making them useful in automating image analysis tasks. When onboard planetary rovers, such capabilities enable the systems to generate contextually relevant metadata in real-time, hereby transforming the passive data acquisition into an active search for predefined scientific phenomena of interest.

Addressing this gap, we introduce the Scientific Prominence Active Search System (SPASS), a novel framework that leverages deep image captioning networks to enhance the autonomy of planetary rovers. The system seamlessly integrates onto existing rover platforms, enabling a shift from traditional deterministic imaging schedules toward a dynamic, content-driven operation. SPASS is designed to caption captured images autonomously and prioritize them for transmission based on their relevance to predefined scientific tasks. By allowing scientists to define search tasks in natural language, SPASS aligns image analysis with the ongoing and evolving priorities of the scientific community, thus ensuring that the most scientifically pertinent data is relayed back to Earth for further investigation.

The research questions guiding our inquiry with SPASS are twofold: How can existing deep captioning networks be adapted for efficient onboard processing on Mars rovers, and how can these captioning results be quantitatively evaluated against predefined scientific specifications? Addressing these questions involves optimizing the network to function under the real-time and computational constraints of onboard rover systems. Additionally, it requires a robust metric for comparing auto-generated captions to task specifications, enabling the efficient selection of images for transmission.

The contributions of our work are threefold. First, we extend the existing deep image captioning networks to suit the unique operational and environmental constraints of Mars rover missions. This involves reducing computational load while maintaining descriptive accuracy. Second, we introduce an adaptive metric for evaluating and matching auto-generated captions against scientist-defined search tasks. This metric facilitates intelligent prioritization of captured images, enhancing the effectiveness of data transmission. Lastly, the SPASS framework is designed to have dual uses - while primarily benefiting Mars rover missions, it can also serve as a ground-based content-oriented search engine, effectively aiding the curation and analysis of the expansive historical datasets already archived in planetary data system repositories.

In summary, SPASS seeks to revolutionize data collection in planetary exploration by empowering rovers with enhanced autonomy through the integration of AI-driven image captioning. This system exemplifies the growing symbiotic relationship between space exploration and artificial intelligence, addressing current limitations while paving the way for more efficient and automated exploration of Mars and beyond. Through SPASS, we can expect not only to improve the rate at which we acquire pertinent data but also to illuminate the pathways toward future autonomous robotic explorers.

Methods

In developing the Scientific Prominence Active Search System (SPASS) with a Deep Image Captioning Network, the research team integrated innovative techniques across varying domains to ensure the accurate identification and prioritization of scientific features in planetary exploration missions. This section delineates the methodologies employed in data management, system design, procedural execution, and statistical analysis utilized to evaluate the effectiveness of SPASS.

Data Collection

The primary dataset for this study comprised existing Mars rover imagery, totaling over 22 million images archived by NASA’s Mars mission. These images were selected based on their diverse representation of geological and atmospheric conditions encountered on Mars. Each image was accompanied by metadata detailing the altitude, geographical location, and timestamp of capture, offering critical contextual data. The dataset served a dual purpose: training the deep image captioning network and validating the search system's performance (Brogan et al., 2021).

The Mars rover images were pre-processed to ensure uniformity in input quality. The pre-processing involved resizing images to a standard resolution conducive for deep learning applications and normalizing pixel values to enhance feature detection capabilities. This step mitigated issues arising from variabilities in image capture conditions such as lighting and rover positioning (Johnson et al., 2019).

System Design

SPASS comprises two primary components: the deep image captioning network and the search prioritization system. The image captioning network was designed using a convolutional neural network (CNN) architecture in conjunction with a recurrent neural network (RNN) layer, achieving a composite framework known for its efficacy in image feature extraction and sequence prediction (Vinyals et al., 2015).
